items.questionText: Under ____ legislation, employers must give at least four weeks' notice of any change to shift patterns.
items.explanation: 'Current' means 'in force at the present time' — the sense Catalan/Spanish 'actual' carries, which is precisely why learners misuse English 'actual' here. English 'actual' would mean 'real as opposed to supposed', 'topical' means 'of present interest in the news', and 'punctual' concerns arriving on time.

items.questionText: The magazine prides itself on essays that are consistently ____, addressing whatever happens to be dominating the news that month.
items.explanation: 'Topical' means 'relating to matters of current public interest' — note it does not mean 'about a topic', which is how Spanish 'tópico' misleads (that word actually means 'cliché'). 'Current' would describe the essays' existence now rather than their subject matter, 'actual' means genuine, and 'punctual' is about timekeeping.

items.questionText: He was unfailingly ____, arriving at every meeting a good five minutes before it was due to begin.
items.explanation: 'Punctual' is the one option in this set that concerns time-keeping, and Spanish 'puntual' is a partial false friend: it also means 'one-off, isolated' (un caso puntual), a sense English never has. 'Actual' means real, 'current' means present-day, and 'topical' means newsworthy.

items.questionText: Two junior researchers were brought in to ____ the professor with the fieldwork.
items.explanation: English 'assist' means 'to help', and takes a person as its object — the exact meaning Spanish 'asistir' does NOT have when it means 'to attend'. Here helping is required, so 'assist' is right; 'attend' would mean being present at, 'assess' means to evaluate, and 'attain' means to reach or achieve.

items.questionText: Examiners are trained to ____ every script against the same published criteria.
items.explanation: 'Assess' means to judge the quality or value of something by measured criteria. 'Attend' means to be present at, 'assist' means to help (the false friend of 'asistir'), and 'attain' means to reach a level — you attain a grade, but the examiner assesses the work that earns it.

items.questionText: Very few candidates ____ the highest band in the speaking paper.
items.explanation: 'Attain' means to reach or achieve something after effort, and collocates naturally with levels, grades and standards. 'Attend' means to be present at, 'assist' means to help, and 'assess' is what the examiner does to the performance rather than what the candidate does to the grade.

items.questionText: It would be far more ____ to postpone the crossing until the wind drops.
items.explanation: English 'sensible' means 'showing good judgement' (Spanish/Catalan 'sensato'), which is what a prudent decision requires. The trap is that Spanish 'sensible' means 'sensitive', the option immediately beside it; 'conscious' means awake or aware, and 'conscientious' means diligent.

items.questionText: The patient remained ____ throughout the procedure, which was carried out under a local anaesthetic.
items.explanation: 'Conscious' means awake and aware of one's surroundings. Spanish 'consciente' spans both this and 'aware that', but the lookalike 'conscientious' means hard-working and thorough — a completely different word. 'Sensitive' and 'sensible' concern feeling and judgement respectively.

items.questionText: A ____ student, she checked every single reference before submitting the essay.
items.explanation: 'Conscientious' means taking care to do one's work thoroughly and properly. Learners reach for 'conscious' because of the shared root and because Spanish 'concienzudo' looks distant; but 'conscious' only means awake or aware. 'Sensitive' means easily affected emotionally, 'sensible' means level-headed.

items.questionText: The inspectors will ____ a full structural survey of the building before any sale proceeds.
items.explanation: 'Carry out' is the standard English rendering of Spanish 'realizar' when it means to perform or execute a task — which is exactly the trap in the original item, where 'realise' was needed instead. 'Realise' in English means to become aware, 'perform' suits duties and artistic works, and 'fulfil' suits obligations and promises.

items.questionText: The quartet will ____ the complete cycle over three consecutive evenings.
items.explanation: 'Perform' is the verb for presenting a work before an audience. 'Carry out' would suit an instruction or a survey but sounds absurd of music, 'realise' means to become aware (not Spanish 'realizar'), and 'fulfil' belongs with duties and conditions.

items.questionText: The council was found to have failed to ____ its statutory duty to rehouse the family.
items.explanation: 'Fulfil' collocates with duties, obligations, promises and conditions — things one is bound to satisfy. 'Carry out' fits tasks and orders, 'perform' fits works and functions, and 'realise' means to become aware, not Spanish 'realizar'.

items.questionText: A postponement at this stage ____ the entire fixture list into confusion.
items.explanation: The fixed collocation is 'throw something into confusion/disarray'. 'Cast' collocates with doubt, light and aspersions; 'put' would need a different frame ('put the schedule in doubt'); and 'lay' collocates with foundations and blame, not confusion.

items.questionText: The revised estimate ____ the total cost of the refurbishment at just under twelve million.
items.explanation: 'Put something at' plus a figure is the set frame for stating an estimate. 'Cast' works with doubt rather than numbers, 'throw' has no such quantifying use, and 'lay' would require an object like 'the blame' or 'the groundwork'.

items.questionText: The opening chapter ____ the groundwork for the argument developed across the rest of the book.
items.explanation: 'Lay the groundwork' (and 'lay the foundations') is fixed — the verb suggests placing something down as a base. 'Cast' pairs with doubt or light, 'throw' with confusion, and 'put' would need an entirely different structure here.

items.questionText: The façade looks like weathered marble, but it is ____ painted plaster.
items.explanation: English 'actually' means 'in reality, contrary to what one might think'. Catalan/Spanish 'actualmente' means 'currently', which is why learners avoid the correct word here. 'Eventually' means in the end, 'punctually' concerns time-keeping, and 'occasionally' means from time to time.

items.questionText: The ceremony began ____ at eleven, exactly as the printed programme had promised.
items.explanation: 'Punctually' means at precisely the appointed time. 'Eventually' means after a long delay — the opposite implication — 'actually' means in fact, and 'occasionally' means now and then. Note that Spanish 'puntualmente' can also mean 'on isolated occasions', a sense English lacks entirely.

items.questionText: He still writes ____, though nothing like as prolifically as he did in his twenties.
items.explanation: 'Occasionally' means from time to time, at irregular and infrequent intervals. 'Eventually' means finally, 'actually' means in reality, and 'punctually' means on time — none of which expresses frequency.

items.questionText: The bank ____ to extend the overdraft, despite thirty years of unbroken custom.
items.explanation: 'Refuse to do something' is the blunt rejection of a request or course of action. 'Deny' rejects the truth of an accusation, not a request — the two are not interchangeable, though Spanish 'negarse a' covers both. 'Decline' is the polite variant, and 'negate' means to nullify.

items.questionText: She ____ the invitation with great courtesy, pleading a long-standing prior engagement.
items.explanation: 'Decline' is the formal, polite refusal of an offer or invitation — the register the adverbial phrase here demands. 'Refuse' would be blunter, 'deny' would mean asserting the invitation never existed, and 'negate' means to cancel out.

items.questionText: A single moment of carelessness ____ an hour of disciplined defending.
items.explanation: 'Negate' means to nullify or cancel out the effect of something. It is not the verb for rejecting a statement, which is 'deny' — Spanish 'negar' covers both, and that overlap is the trap. 'Refuse' and 'decline' both reject offers rather than undo effects.

items.questionText: The last independent ____ on the high street closed after forty years of trading.
items.explanation: A 'bookshop' sells books; a 'library' lends them. Spanish 'librería' and Catalan 'llibreria' mean the shop, while 'biblioteca' means the library — the crossover that makes this one of the most persistent false friends of all. 'Stationer's' sells paper and pens; a 'newsagent's' sells papers.

items.questionText: I called in at the ____ for a box of envelopes and some index cards.
items.explanation: A 'stationer's' sells writing materials — paper, envelopes, pens. Note the spelling: 'stationery' with an 'e' is the goods, 'stationary' with an 'a' means motionless. A 'library' lends books, a 'bookshop' sells them, and a 'newsagent's' deals in newspapers.

items.questionText: He picked up a paper from the ____ on the corner every morning without fail.
items.explanation: A 'newsagent's' is the shop selling newspapers, magazines and tobacco — Spanish 'quiosco'. A 'library' lends books, a 'bookshop' sells them, and a 'stationer's' sells writing materials; only one of the four deals in the daily press.

items.questionText: The committee ____ a series of detailed recommendations that the board promptly ignored.
items.explanation: 'Make a recommendation' is fixed; the delexicalised verb is chosen by the noun, not by logic. Spanish uses 'hacer' for many of these, but English distributes them across 'make', 'do' and 'take', so each collocation must be learned. 'Carry out' suits research and orders, 'take' suits decisions and steps, and 'realise' means to become aware.

items.questionText: The negotiations ____ the better part of a fortnight to conclude.
items.explanation: 'Take' is the verb English uses for the consumption of time. 'Make' pairs with recommendations and decisions of a different kind, 'carry out' pairs with research and instructions, and 'realise' means to become aware — Spanish 'realizar' is the false friend that pulls learners towards it.

items.questionText: Only when the auditors arrived did the directors ____ quite how serious the shortfall had become.
items.explanation: English 'realise' means to become aware of something — 'darse cuenta'. The interference runs the other way here: Spanish 'realizar' means to carry out, so learners avoid 'realise' in exactly the context where it belongs. 'Made', 'took' and 'carried out' are all delexical verbs of performance, not perception.

items.questionText: The original joists are nowhere near strong enough to ____ the weight of the new machinery.
items.explanation: 'Support' means to bear weight from below, or to back a cause. What it does not mean is 'to tolerate', which is where Spanish 'soportar' misleads — that sense is 'bear', 'stand' or 'put up with'. 'Withstand' means to resist damage, 'sustain' means to keep going, and 'hold' means to contain.

items.questionText: The runner ____ a serious hamstring injury in the closing stages of the race.
items.explanation: 'Sustain an injury' is the formal collocation for suffering one — a use that surprises learners who know 'sustain' only as 'maintain'. 'Withstand' means to resist without giving way, 'support' means to bear weight, and 'hold' means to contain.

items.questionText: The reservoir can ____ enough water to supply the whole city for a fortnight.
items.explanation: 'Hold' here means to have the capacity to contain. 'Withstand' means to survive an assault or extreme, 'support' means to bear weight from beneath, and 'sustain' means to keep something going over time — the reservoir's capacity is a matter of volume, not endurance.

items.questionText: Her supervisor was remarkably ____ about the delay, given how tight the deadline had been.
items.explanation: 'Understanding' as an adjective describes a person who is sympathetic and forgiving towards others' difficulties. 'Comprehensive' means complete in scope — the false friend of Spanish 'comprensivo', which means precisely 'understanding'. 'Perceptive' means quick to notice, 'considerate' means thoughtful of others' comfort.

items.questionText: It was a ____ remark, and one that went straight to the heart of the difficulty.
items.explanation: 'Perceptive' means showing keen insight and quick understanding of something subtle. 'Comprehensive' means covering everything, 'understanding' describes sympathy towards people rather than acuteness of mind, and 'considerate' means attentive to others' comfort.

items.questionText: It was extremely ____ of them to keep the noise down while the baby was sleeping.
items.explanation: 'Considerate' means showing regard for other people's feelings and comfort. 'Understanding' implies sympathy with a difficulty, 'perceptive' implies sharpness of insight, and 'comprehensive' means exhaustive in coverage — the last being the false friend of 'comprensivo'.

items.questionText: The gallery is ____ closed for refurbishment and will reopen in the spring.
items.explanation: 'Currently' means at the present time — the meaning Catalan/Spanish 'actualment/actualmente' carries, and the reason learners write 'actually' when they mean this. English 'actually' means 'in fact', 'presently' most often means 'soon', and 'nowadays' contrasts the present era with the past.

items.questionText: If you would care to take a seat, the consultant will see you ____.
items.explanation: 'Presently' in this frame means 'shortly, before long' — its dominant British sense with a future verb. 'Currently' would state a present state rather than a coming event, 'actually' means in reality, and 'nowadays' sets the present age against former times.

items.questionText: Hardly anyone bothers to have film developed ____, now that everything is shot digitally.
items.explanation: 'Nowadays' contrasts the present era with an earlier one, which is exactly what the clause about digital photography sets up. 'Currently' states a temporary present state without that historical contrast, 'actually' means in fact, and 'presently' means soon.

items.questionText: The tribunal was broadly ____ to her account, but found it insufficiently corroborated.
items.explanation: English 'sympathetic' means showing understanding of, or favour towards, someone's position. Spanish/Catalan 'simpático' means 'likeable', which is the false friend at work in the original item. 'Likeable' describes charm, 'sensible' means level-headed, and 'comprehensive' means complete in scope.

items.questionText: Wearing ____ shoes for a walk of that length turned out to be a wise precaution.
items.explanation: 'Sensible' in English means practical and showing good judgement — 'sensato'. Spanish 'sensible' means 'sensitive', which is the trap. 'Likeable' describes a person's appeal, 'sympathetic' means understanding towards someone, and 'comprehensive' means all-inclusive.

items.questionText: The manual is admirably ____, covering every fault the machine is ever likely to develop.
items.explanation: 'Comprehensive' means complete, leaving nothing out. It is the false friend of Spanish 'comprensivo' ('understanding') and must also be kept apart from 'comprehensible' ('able to be understood'). 'Likeable', 'sympathetic' and 'sensible' all describe people rather than coverage.

items.questionText: The legislation was never ____ to cover charitable bodies of this kind.
items.explanation: 'Intend' means to have as one's purpose or design. The trap runs in both directions: Spanish 'pretender' means 'to intend', while English 'pretend' means to feign — so learners routinely swap them. 'Expected' concerns anticipation, 'aspired' concerns ambition.

items.questionText: Turnout on the day was far lower than anyone at party headquarters had ____.
items.explanation: 'Expect' means to regard something as likely to happen. 'Intend' concerns purpose rather than prediction, 'pretend' means to feign (the false friend of 'pretender'), and 'aspire' means to direct one's ambition towards something.

items.questionText: She had always ____ to a chair in classics, and finally secured one at sixty.
items.explanation: 'Aspire to' means to direct one's ambition towards a position or goal, and takes 'to' rather than a direct object. 'Intended' states a plan, 'expected' states an anticipation, and 'pretended' means feigned — not Spanish 'pretender', which means to intend.

items.questionText: The gallery ____ its winter exhibition on hoardings right across the city.
items.explanation: 'Advertise' means to publicise something commercially. Spanish 'advertir' means 'to warn', so the pair is a two-way trap: 'advertise' never warns, and the original item needed 'warn'. 'Advise' means to counsel, and 'notify' means to inform officially.

items.questionText: Counsel ____ the client to settle rather than risk an adverse costs order.
items.explanation: 'Advise' means to recommend a course of action, and takes 'someone to do something'. 'Warn' would stress danger, 'advertise' means to promote publicly (not Spanish 'advertir'), and 'notify' is the neutral verb for giving formal notice.

items.questionText: The system automatically ____ the registrar of any change of address.
items.explanation: 'Notify someone of something' is the formal collocation for giving official information. 'Warn' implies danger, 'advise' implies a recommendation, and 'advertise' implies commercial promotion — only 'notify' is purely informational.

items.questionText: Counsel for the defence will ____ that the search was unlawful from the outset.
items.explanation: 'Argue that' means to advance a reasoned case for a proposition — a neutral, formal use with no suggestion of a row. 'Discuss' means to talk something over, 'dispute' means to challenge the truth of something, and 'quarrel' means to fall out angrily.

items.questionText: Few historians would seriously ____ the significance of the treaty for the region.
items.explanation: 'Dispute' means to call into question or contest the truth of a claim. 'Discuss' is neutral talk (Spanish 'discutir' means to argue, which is exactly the interference this set targets), 'argue' means to reason for a position, and 'quarrel' means to fall out.

items.questionText: The two brothers continued to ____ over the estate for the better part of a decade.
items.explanation: 'Quarrel' means to have a prolonged angry disagreement, usually personal — the strongest and least formal option here. 'Discuss' is calm and neutral, 'argue' can be purely intellectual, and 'dispute' contests a specific claim rather than souring a relationship.

items.questionText: An endorsement from the outgoing chair would ____ considerable weight with the selection panel.
items.explanation: 'Carry weight' is the fixed idiom for being influential. 'Bear the brunt' is a different fixed frame meaning to absorb the worst of something, 'take' would need its own collocate, and 'suffer' requires a hardship rather than an abstract quantity of influence.

items.questionText: Delegates were invited to ____ their seats before the afternoon session resumed.
items.explanation: 'Take one's seat' is fixed: English selects the delexical verb by collocation, not by logic, which is why Spanish speakers who generalise 'coger/tomar' still have to learn each pairing. 'Bear' means to endure or support, 'carry' means to convey, and 'suffer' requires something unpleasant.

items.questionText: The region continues to ____ from decades of chronic underinvestment in public transport.
items.explanation: 'Suffer from' is the frame for enduring an ongoing affliction, and the preposition settles it: none of the other three takes 'from' in this sense. 'Bear' takes a direct object such as 'the brunt', 'carry' means to convey, and 'take' would need its own fixed collocate.

items.questionText: The composer died in poverty and remained almost entirely ____ for the better part of a century.
items.explanation: 'Forgotten' means no longer remembered. The other three share the 'fore-' prefix of anticipation: 'foregone' means settled in advance, 'forthcoming' means about to occur or willing to give information, and 'forecast' means predicted.

items.questionText: Ministers proved notably less ____ about the cost of the scheme than about its supposed benefits.
items.explanation: 'Forthcoming' has two senses; here it is 'willing to divulge information', the one learners rarely meet. 'Foregone' belongs only to 'a foregone conclusion', 'forgotten' means lost to memory, and 'forecast' means predicted in advance.

items.questionText: Growth had been ____ at three per cent, but the eventual outturn was barely half that.
items.explanation: 'Forecast' means predicted on the basis of data, and its past participle is unchanged. 'Foregone' means already decided, 'forgotten' means no longer remembered, and 'forthcoming' means imminent or open — none of which reports a numerical projection.

items.questionText: The public gallery sat ____ as the verdict was read out.
items.explanation: 'Mute' means silent, saying nothing. It is a near-homophone of 'moot', which means debatable or academic, and the two are constantly confused in writing. 'Mood' is a noun meaning a state of feeling, and 'moored' means tied up at a berth.

items.questionText: There was no mistaking the ____ of the meeting once the revised figures had been circulated.
items.explanation: 'Mood' is a noun denoting a prevailing feeling or atmosphere, and only a noun will follow 'the' here. 'Moot' is an adjective meaning open to debate, 'mute' means silent, and 'moored' means secured at a mooring.

items.questionText: The vessel lay ____ at the quayside for the better part of a winter.
items.explanation: 'Moored' means secured to a fixed point by rope or anchor. The three lookalikes are unrelated: 'moot' means arguable, 'mute' means silent, and 'mood' is a noun of atmosphere — a classic C2 set testing spelling discrimination rather than meaning alone.

items.questionText: The chancellor pointedly declined to rule out a rise in the basic rate of ____.
items.explanation: 'Tax' is a compulsory levy imposed by the state on income or goods. A 'toll' is a charge for using a road or bridge (and, figuratively, a cost in damage), a 'fee' is a payment for a service, and 'cost' is what something amounts to overall.

items.questionText: Applicants must pay a non-refundable ____ of forty pounds when submitting the form.
items.explanation: A 'fee' is a fixed charge for a professional service or administrative process. A 'tax' is levied by the state on income or transactions, a 'toll' is charged for passage, and 'cost' denotes the total outlay rather than a set charge.

items.questionText: The stadium was eventually completed at a ____ of nearly twelve million pounds.
items.explanation: 'At a cost of' is the fixed frame for reporting total expenditure. 'Toll' would be figurative damage and does not take this frame, 'tax' is a state levy, and 'fee' is a charge for a specific service.

items.questionText: The referee's decision was a close ____, though the replays suggested he had got it right.
items.explanation: 'A close call' means a narrowly decided or narrowly avoided outcome. 'A far cry from' expresses distance between two states, 'a long shot' means an unlikely attempt, and 'a long way from' expresses remaining distance — each idiom is locked to its own adjective.

items.questionText: Applying for the fellowship was a long ____, but to everyone's astonishment it came off.
items.explanation: 'A long shot' is an attempt with little chance of success. The adjective is what fixes the idiom: 'a long way' expresses distance, 'a far cry' expresses contrast, and 'a close call' expresses narrowness — swap the adjective and the idiom collapses.

items.questionText: The prototype is still a long ____ from being ready for commercial production.
items.explanation: 'A long way from' states how much remains to be covered. 'A far cry from' would need 'far', not 'long', and stresses contrast with a former state; 'a close call' and 'a long shot' concern narrow margins and poor odds respectively.

items.questionText: Her position as both auditor and shareholder created an obvious ____ of interest.
items.explanation: 'Conflict of interest' is a fixed technical phrase for incompatible duties. 'A bone of contention' is the idiom for a recurring subject of argument, 'in dispute' means formally contested, and 'discord' denotes a lack of harmony between people.

items.questionText: Ownership of the land has been in ____ between the two families since the 1920s.
items.explanation: 'In dispute' means formally contested, typically in law. 'Contention' appears in 'a bone of contention' and in 'in contention' meaning 'still in the running' — a different sense entirely; 'conflict' needs 'of interest' or an armed context, and 'discord' describes strained relations, not a legal status.

items.questionText: A note of ____ crept into the coalition almost as soon as it had been formed.
items.explanation: 'Discord' means disagreement and lack of harmony, and 'a note of discord' borrows the musical metaphor. 'Contention' belongs to 'a bone of contention', 'conflict' to 'of interest' or to warfare, and 'dispute' to formally contested matters.

items.questionText: Counsel rose to raise a formal ____ to the admission of the recording.
items.explanation: You 'raise an objection' — the verb is what fixes this one. 'Take exception to' is the idiom for being offended, 'take offence at' is its blunter cousin, and 'take issue with' means to disagree openly; each requires its own verb and preposition.

items.questionText: He took considerable ____ at being asked to justify every item of expenditure.
items.explanation: 'Take offence at' is fixed, and the preposition decides it: 'take exception' requires 'to', and 'take issue' requires 'with'. 'Objection' pairs with 'raise' rather than 'take' — a set of idioms where the preposition carries the whole answer.

items.questionText: The auditors took ____ with the valuation placed on the intangible assets.
items.explanation: 'Take issue with' means to disagree openly with a claim or figure. 'Take exception to' means to be offended by, 'take offence at' likewise, and 'raise an objection' uses a different verb altogether — the prepositions 'with', 'to' and 'at' keep them apart.

items.questionText: Winning the away leg took the side up a ____ in everyone's estimation.
items.explanation: 'Up a notch' means by one clear step or degree. 'Up to scratch' means meeting the required standard, 'make the grade' means to succeed in reaching it, and 'at ministerial level' locates a rank — four idioms of standard that are not interchangeable.

items.questionText: He never quite made the ____ at international level and returned to the domestic game.
items.explanation: 'Make the grade' means to reach the necessary standard. 'Up to scratch' expresses the same idea adjectivally but cannot follow 'make', 'up a notch' means one degree better, and 'level' would need a preposition such as 'at'.

items.questionText: Talks are expected to resume at ministerial ____ towards the end of the month.
items.explanation: 'At ministerial level' denotes the rank at which something happens. 'Scratch' works only in 'up to scratch' or 'from scratch', 'notch' only in 'up a notch', and 'grade' only in 'make the grade' — all four are locked into distinct frames.

items.questionText: Through a gap in the hedge she ____ a fox slipping silently across the lawn.
items.explanation: 'Glimpse' means to see something briefly and incompletely, often by chance — the emphasis is on what was seen. 'Glance' emphasises the brief look itself, 'peer' means to look hard at something difficult to make out, and 'gaze' means to look long and steadily.

items.questionText: He ____ over his spectacles at the figures printed on the final page.
items.explanation: 'Peer' means to look with concentrated effort at something hard to see. 'Glance' is quick and casual, 'glimpse' is about catching sight of something momentarily, and 'gaze' implies long, absorbed looking rather than strain.

items.questionText: She ____ out across the estuary for a long while, saying nothing at all.
items.explanation: 'Gaze' means to look steadily and at length, usually in wonder or abstraction — the duration is the point. 'Glance' is momentary, 'glimpse' concerns a fleeting sight of something, and 'peer' implies squinting effort.

items.questionText: A single ____ at the balance sheet was enough to tell him the company was finished.
items.explanation: As a noun, 'a glance at' is a brief deliberate look. 'A glimpse of' is an accidental partial sighting and takes 'of', 'a peek' is a furtive look, and 'a sighting' is a recorded observation of something rare — here the preposition 'at' does much of the work.

items.questionText: The children took a quick ____ behind the curtain while nobody was watching.
items.explanation: 'A peek' is a quick, furtive and usually forbidden look. 'A glance' is brief but open, 'a glimpse' is what you catch rather than what you take, and 'a sighting' is a formal record of having observed something.

items.questionText: The first confirmed ____ of the species in Britain for eighty years was recorded last spring.
items.explanation: 'A sighting' is an instance of observing something rare, treated as a recordable event. 'A glimpse' is fleeting and subjective, 'a glance' is a deliberate brief look, and 'a peek' is furtive — none of them can be 'confirmed' and logged.

items.questionText: The complainants ____ that the firm knowingly overstated its reserves for three years running.
items.explanation: 'Allege' means to assert without yet providing proof, and carries a strong implication that the claim is unproven. 'Maintain' means to keep insisting on one's own position, 'assert' means to state forcefully, and 'contend' means to argue a case against opposition.

items.questionText: The author does not merely ____ the claim; he documents it painstakingly across three chapters.
items.explanation: 'Assert' means to state something confidently as fact — the contrast with 'documents' is what makes it fit, since asserting is precisely stating without demonstrating. 'Allege' implies an accusation, 'maintain' implies persistence under challenge, and 'contend' implies argument against an opponent.

items.questionText: Sceptics ____ that the correlation is no more than an artefact of the sampling method.
items.explanation: 'Contend' means to argue a position against competing views — the presence of sceptics supplies exactly that opposition. 'Allege' implies an unproven accusation, 'assert' is a bare confident statement, and 'maintain' stresses holding to a position over time.

items.questionText: Throughout the hearing he ____ that he had acted entirely on legal advice.
items.explanation: 'Maintain' means to continue to insist on something in the face of challenge, which the duration of a hearing supplies. 'Allege' would accuse someone else without proof, 'assert' is a single confident statement, and 'confide' means to tell in private.

items.questionText: The paper ____ its central claim with a confidence its evidence did not really warrant.
items.explanation: 'Assert' means to state something firmly as though it needed no support — hence the mismatch with the evidence. 'Maintain' implies holding a line under pressure, 'allege' implies an unproven accusation, and 'confide' implies a private disclosure.

items.questionText: She ____ to a trusted colleague that she was seriously thinking of resigning.
items.explanation: 'Confide' means to tell someone something private in confidence, and takes 'to' before the hearer. 'Allege', 'assert' and 'maintain' are all public acts of claiming, and none carries the sense of entrusting a secret.

items.questionText: The indictment ____ that the funds were routed through three shell companies in succession.
items.explanation: 'Allege' is the formal verb for a charge that is asserted but not yet proved — precisely the status of anything in an indictment. 'Contend' argues a case, 'divulge' reveals a secret, and 'profess' claims a feeling or belief, often insincerely.

items.questionText: The memoir ____ almost nothing about the years he spent in government.
items.explanation: 'Divulge' means to reveal information that was previously secret. 'Allege' makes an unproven accusation, 'contend' argues a position, and 'profess' declares a belief or feeling — only 'divulge' concerns the release of withheld information.

items.questionText: He ____ complete indifference to the prize, though almost nobody believes him.
items.explanation: 'Profess' means to claim a feeling or belief openly, very often with a hint that the claim is hollow — which the concessive clause confirms. 'Allege' accuses, 'contend' argues, and 'divulge' discloses fact rather than feeling.

items.questionText: Passenger safety is ____ and must override every commercial consideration.
items.explanation: 'Paramount' means supreme, more important than anything else. 'Tantamount' means equivalent in effect and always takes 'to', 'surmount' is a verb meaning to overcome, and 'amount' as a verb means to add up to — a set of near-homophones with quite unrelated jobs.

items.questionText: The team had one final procedural obstacle to ____ before qualification was assured.
items.explanation: 'Surmount' is a verb meaning to overcome a difficulty, and only a verb can follow 'to' here. 'Paramount' is an adjective meaning supreme, 'tantamount' an adjective meaning equivalent to, and 'amount' would require 'to' plus a quantity.

items.questionText: The fines ____ to considerably less than the profit the company made from the breach.
items.explanation: 'Amount to' means to add up to a total. 'Tantamount to' looks similar and also takes 'to', but it means 'equivalent in effect to' and is an adjective, so it cannot follow 'The fines' directly. 'Paramount' means supreme and 'surmount' means to overcome.

items.questionText: The drug was withdrawn after a cluster of ____ reactions was reported across three hospitals.
items.explanation: 'Adverse' means harmful or unfavourable and modifies things — conditions, reactions, publicity. 'Averse' means disinclined, describes people and always takes 'to'; the pair differ by a single letter and are among the most frequently confused adjectives in formal English. 'Reluctant' and 'hostile' also describe attitudes, not effects.

items.questionText: She was distinctly ____ to commit herself before she had seen the final draft.
items.explanation: 'Reluctant to do something' expresses unwillingness about a specific act. 'Averse to' expresses a settled distaste and normally takes a noun or gerund, 'adverse' means harmful and cannot describe a person, and 'hostile' implies active opposition rather than hesitancy.

items.questionText: The proposal met with a frankly ____ reception from all three of the unions involved.
items.explanation: 'Hostile' means actively antagonistic — far stronger than mere unwillingness. 'Averse' means disinclined and needs 'to', 'reluctant' means hesitant, and 'adverse' means unfavourable in effect, which would describe consequences rather than a reception.

items.questionText: The trestle tables were ____ with far more food than the guests could conceivably eat.
items.explanation: 'Laden with' means physically loaded down with something, and is the only one of the four that suits a positive abundance of goods. 'Fraught with' is reserved for danger and difficulty, 'riddled with' for faults and holes, and 'rife' takes no object at all in this pattern.

items.questionText: The final draft was ____ with factual errors that nobody had troubled to check.
items.explanation: 'Riddled with' means pervaded by something bad that has spread throughout — errors, corruption, woodworm. 'Fraught with' pairs specifically with risk and difficulty, 'laden with' implies a physical load, and 'rife' is used predicatively without 'with'.

items.questionText: Rumours of an imminent takeover were ____ in the City throughout that summer.
items.explanation: 'Rife' means widespread and is used predicatively, without a following 'with' when the subject is the thing spreading. 'Fraught', 'laden' and 'riddled' all require 'with' plus the thing that fills the subject, so none of them fits this structure.

items.questionText: Evidence of early settlement is ____ throughout the lower reaches of the valley.
items.explanation: 'Abundant' means existing in large quantities, and collocates strongly with 'evidence'. 'Rife' is almost always negative and describes the spread of something unwelcome, 'plentiful' suits supplies and opportunities, and 'copious' suits quantities produced or recorded.

items.questionText: Jobs were ____ in the boom years, and wages rose steadily as a result.
items.explanation: 'Plentiful' means available in more than sufficient quantity, and is the natural adjective for supplies of work, food or money. 'Rife' would imply something undesirable spreading, 'abundant' collocates with evidence and natural resources, and 'copious' with amounts produced.

items.questionText: She took ____ notes throughout the three days of the hearing.
items.explanation: 'Copious notes' is a fixed collocation: 'copious' describes something produced in great quantity. 'Rife' means widespread in a negative sense, 'abundant' pairs with evidence and resources, and 'plentiful' with supply — neither of the last two is used of notes.

items.questionText: The escaped prisoner remained ____ for a further three weeks before being recaptured.
items.explanation: 'At large' means still free and uncaptured. 'By and large' means generally speaking, 'at length' means for a long time or at last, and 'by far' intensifies a superlative — four phrases built from the same handful of words with entirely separate jobs.

items.questionText: She spoke ____ about the failings of the previous administration before taking any questions.
items.explanation: 'At length' here means for a long time and in detail. 'By and large' means on the whole, 'at large' means still at liberty, and 'by far' modifies a superlative — the preposition alone will not tell you which; the whole phrase must be learned as a unit.

items.questionText: This is ____ the most ambitious project the studio has ever attempted.
items.explanation: 'By far' intensifies a superlative and can only appear with one. 'By and large' means generally, 'at large' means uncaptured or, after a noun, 'in general' (the public at large), and 'at length' means at long duration.

items.questionText: The committee chose to postpone the decision ____ risk a damaging split vote.
items.explanation: 'Rather than' expresses a preference between two courses of action and readily takes a bare infinitive. 'Let alone' introduces something even less likely after a negative, 'instead of' takes a noun or gerund, and 'as well as' adds rather than replaces.

items.questionText: He sent a brief note ____ attending the meeting in person as he had promised.
items.explanation: 'Instead of' marks a substitution and is followed by a noun or an -ing form. 'Let alone' needs a preceding negative and escalates, 'rather than' expresses preference, and 'as well as' adds a second item rather than replacing the first.

items.questionText: The grant covers travel ____ accommodation for the full duration of the placement.
items.explanation: 'As well as' is additive: both items are covered. 'Instead of' would mean one replaced the other, 'rather than' would express a preference, and 'let alone' would require a negative and would reverse the sense entirely.

items.questionText: The magistrates were plainly ____ to his circumstances, yet felt bound by the sentencing guidelines.
items.explanation: 'Sympathetic to' means understanding of and inclined to favour someone's position. Spanish/Catalan 'simpàtic/simpático' means 'likeable', which is the interference this quartet is built on. 'Sensible' means level-headed, and 'compromising' means damaging to one's reputation.

items.questionText: Postponing the launch seemed the only ____ course of action in the circumstances.
items.explanation: English 'sensible' means showing sound judgement — 'sensato'. The trap is that Spanish 'sensible' means 'sensitive', a meaning English 'sensible' never has. 'Likeable' describes personal appeal, 'sympathetic' describes understanding of others, and 'compromising' describes incriminating material.

items.questionText: The photographs were sufficiently ____ to end his political career within a fortnight.
items.explanation: 'Compromising' means revealing something discreditable — it does not mean 'willing to make concessions', which is where Spanish 'comprometido/compromís' misleads. 'Likeable' and 'sympathetic' describe how a person is regarded, and 'sensible' means prudent.

items.questionText: The entire customer database had been ____ within hours of the initial breach.
items.explanation: 'Compromise' in this sense means to expose to danger or unauthorised access. Spanish 'comprometerse' means to commit oneself, which is the false friend the original item exploits: 'pledge' is the verb for a public promise. 'Engage' means to hire or occupy, and 'consent' means to give permission.

items.questionText: The board ____ a specialist consultant to review its safety procedures from top to bottom.
items.explanation: 'Engage' in formal register means to hire someone for professional services. Spanish 'compromiso' covers both 'commitment' and 'engagement', which blurs this set for learners. 'Pledge' means to promise publicly, 'compromise' means to expose to risk or to settle by concession, and 'consent' means to permit.

items.questionText: The patient had not ____ to the particular procedure that was eventually performed.
items.explanation: 'Consent to' means to give formal permission, and the preposition 'to' plus a procedure fixes it. 'Pledge' promises a future action, 'compromise' means to endanger or to meet halfway, and 'engage' means to hire or to occupy.

items.questionText: Quarterly sales are expected to ____ a new record before the end of the year.
items.explanation: 'Hit a record' is the standard collocation for reaching a peak figure. 'Strike' pairs with 'a balance', 'a deal' and 'a chord' but never with records, 'beat' would require a rival or a previous mark as its object, and 'touch' is not used of figures in this way.

items.questionText: No visiting side has managed to ____ them on their own ground for eleven months.
items.explanation: 'Beat' means to defeat an opponent and takes the opponent as its object. 'Strike' would need one of its fixed nouns such as 'a balance', 'hit' means to reach or to strike physically, and 'touch' means to make contact with or, idiomatically, to equal in quality.

items.questionText: He has scarcely ____ his food all evening, which is quite unlike him.
items.explanation: 'Touch one's food' is the idiomatic way of saying one has not eaten any of it, and only 'touch' works in the negative frame. 'Strike a balance' is a fixed phrase of a different kind, 'hit' implies force, and 'beat' implies defeating something.

items.questionText: The witness was far too distressed to give a ____ account of what had actually happened.
items.explanation: 'Coherent' means logically ordered and intelligible in itself. 'Consistent' means free from contradiction, usually measured against something else and taking 'with'; 'concordant' is a technical term for agreement between paired observations; and 'corresponding' means matching a counterpart.

items.questionText: In twin studies the pair were described as ____ for the condition, both having developed it before thirty.
items.explanation: 'Concordant for' is the technical term in twin research for both members sharing a trait — a genuinely restricted use that no other option can take. 'Consistent' would need 'with', 'coherent' describes internal logic, and 'corresponding' describes a matching counterpart.

items.questionText: Profits rose by nine per cent on the ____ period a year earlier.
items.explanation: 'The corresponding period' is fixed in financial reporting: the equivalent stretch of time in another year. 'Consistent' would need 'with' and means non-contradictory, 'coherent' means internally logical, and 'concordant' is a technical term for paired agreement.

items.questionText: The exhibition attracted a remarkably ____ range of visitors from across the county.
items.explanation: 'A wide range' is the fixed collocation for variety of coverage. 'Sweeping' means drastic and far-reaching, and is used of changes and reforms rather than ranges; 'ample' means more than enough in quantity; and 'broad-minded' describes a tolerant person.

items.questionText: There is ____ evidence that the practice continued for years after the formal ban.
items.explanation: 'Ample evidence' means plentiful and quite sufficient evidence — the collocation is standard in formal argument. 'Sweeping' means drastic in scope, 'wide' would need 'range' or a similar noun, and 'broad-minded' can only describe a person's outlook.

items.questionText: Her parents were unusually ____ for their generation and never once objected.
items.explanation: 'Broad-minded' means tolerant of unfamiliar or unconventional opinions, and applies only to people. 'Sweeping' describes far-reaching changes, 'wide' describes physical or notional extent, and 'ample' describes sufficiency of quantity.

items.questionText: The chamber grew increasingly ____ as members demanded an immediate vote.
items.explanation: 'Clamorous' means noisy and insistently vocal — it is about sound. 'Blatant' means shamelessly obvious and is about conspicuousness, not volume, despite the similar feel; 'notorious' means famous for something bad; and 'evident' simply means apparent.

items.questionText: The junction is ____ for accidents in wet weather, yet nothing has been done about it.
items.explanation: 'Notorious for' means well known for something bad, and the preposition 'for' is part of the pattern. 'Blatant' means brazenly obvious, 'clamorous' means noisy, and 'evident' means plainly visible without any implication of ill repute.

items.questionText: It was ____ from her expression that the news had not been good.
items.explanation: 'Evident' means plain to see, and is neutral in tone. 'Blatant' adds shamelessness to obviousness and would be far too loaded here, 'notorious' means infamous, and 'clamorous' means loudly insistent.

items.questionText: The manuscript is demonstrably ____ to the events it purports to record at first hand.
items.explanation: 'Posterior to' means later in time than — a formal use that takes 'to'. 'Ulterior' means hidden and self-interested (as in 'ulterior motive'), 'exterior' means outer, and only 'posterior' expresses chronological sequence.

items.questionText: The ____ walls were rendered and repainted during the following spring.
items.explanation: 'Exterior' means situated on the outside. 'Ulterior' means concealed and usually self-serving, and survives almost solely in 'ulterior motive'; 'posterior' means later or situated behind. The shared '-erior' ending is the whole trap here.

items.questionText: Negotiations ____ an impasse over the question of pension entitlements.
items.explanation: 'Hit an impasse' (or a snag, or a wall) is the collocation for running into an obstacle. 'Strike' pairs with 'a deal' or 'a balance', 'close' pairs with 'a deal' or 'the bidding', and 'knock' would need a particle such as 'off' or 'down'.

items.questionText: The auctioneer declined to ____ the bidding until the reserve price had been met.
items.explanation: 'Close the bidding' means to bring it formally to an end. 'Strike' collocates with 'a deal' rather than with bidding, 'hit' means to reach or collide with, and 'knock' in an auction context needs 'down' to mean sold.

items.questionText: The revised drawings ____ six weeks off the construction timetable at a stroke.
items.explanation: 'Knock something off' a total means to reduce it by that amount. 'Strike' would need 'a deal' or 'a balance', 'hit' means to reach a figure rather than to remove from one, and 'close' means to bring to an end.

items.questionText: The proposal ____ the technical detail the committee had expressly asked for.
items.explanation: 'Lack' takes a direct object and means simply to be without something. 'Fall short of' is the idiom for failing to reach a standard and needs 'of', 'miss' implies failing to hit a defined target, and 'drop' implies a decline from a previous level.

items.questionText: The department ____ its recycling target for the third consecutive year.
items.explanation: 'Miss a target' is the standard collocation for failing to achieve a stated figure. 'Fall short' expresses the same idea but requires 'of', 'lack' means to be without something rather than to fail to reach it, and 'drop' describes a fall in level.

items.questionText: Attendances ____ sharply once the club raised its season-ticket prices.
items.explanation: 'Drop' means to fall to a lower level, and takes an adverb of degree such as 'sharply'. 'Fall short' needs 'of' plus a target, 'lack' means to be without, and 'miss' requires a specific target to have been missed.

items.questionText: Whole villages were left ____ by the relief effort until the national press arrived.
items.explanation: 'Forgotten' means overlooked or no longer remembered. The other three carry the 'fore-' of anticipation: 'foregone' means settled in advance, 'forthcoming' means about to happen, and 'forewarned' means alerted beforehand.

items.questionText: The society's ____ conference is to be held in Edinburgh over three days in April.
items.explanation: 'Forthcoming' before a noun means about to take place. 'Foregone' occurs almost exclusively in 'a foregone conclusion', 'forgotten' means no longer remembered, and 'forewarned' means warned in advance and cannot modify an event.

items.questionText: The crew, ____ of the approaching storm, had secured everything on deck by dusk.
items.explanation: 'Forewarned of' means alerted to something before it happens. 'Foregone' means already decided, 'forgotten' means no longer remembered, and 'forthcoming' means imminent — only 'forewarned' describes people who have received notice.

items.questionText: The trust had ____ heavily in government bonds in the months before the crash.
items.explanation: 'Invest in' means to put money into something in the hope of return, and the preposition 'in' settles it. 'A vested interest' is a fixed phrase meaning a personal stake that biases one's judgement, 'interested' before 'party' means formally concerned, and neither takes 'in' this way.

items.questionText: Any ____ party may make written representations before the closing date.
items.explanation: 'An interested party' is fixed legal usage for anyone with a formal stake in a matter. 'Vested' appears only in 'a vested interest', and cannot modify 'party'; 'invested' would mean money had been placed somewhere.

items.questionText: She has long been a ____ advocate of open access to publicly funded research.
items.explanation: 'A strong advocate' is the natural collocation for someone who argues forcefully for a cause. 'Drive a hard bargain' is a separate fixed idiom, and 'hard' cannot modify 'advocate'; 'heavy' describes weight, traffic or rain rather than conviction.

items.questionText: Traffic was unusually ____ on the approach to the tunnel that morning.
items.explanation: 'Heavy traffic' is fixed — the adjective for density of flow. 'Hard' belongs to 'drive a hard bargain' and 'hard evidence', 'strong' pairs with advocates, opinions and currencies; neither is used of traffic in standard English.

items.questionText: The college has spent a decade ____ its bursary fund with donations from former students.
items.explanation: 'Augment' means to make something greater by adding to it, and takes a direct object. 'Mounting' is intransitive and describes pressure or tension that builds of its own accord, so it could never take 'its bursary fund' as an object.

items.questionText: The counter keeps ____ by one every time the sensor at the turnstile is triggered.
items.explanation: 'Increment' is a narrowly technical verb meaning to increase by a fixed step, and belongs to computing and measurement rather than to general prose. 'Mounting' describes pressure accumulating steadily and immeasurably, and 'augmenting' means enlarging by addition — neither implies a fixed unit.

items.questionText: She poured the ____ water straight onto the tea leaves and left them to steep.
items.explanation: 'Scalding' means hot enough to burn the skin, and is literal. 'Scathing' means fiercely critical and is used only of words — reports, reviews, remarks — while 'burning' before a noun usually means urgent or intensely felt rather than physically near-boiling.

items.questionText: The ____ question, which nobody at the meeting would address, was how the shortfall would be met.
items.explanation: 'A burning question' is fixed: one that is urgent and demands an answer. 'Scathing' describes savagely critical language, and 'scalding' describes liquid hot enough to injure — the two lookalikes are literal and figurative in quite different directions.

items.questionText: Digitising the archive ____ the department several thousand hours of manual searching.
items.explanation: 'Save' takes a double object — save someone something — when the thing spared is time or effort. 'Cut corners' is a fixed idiom meaning to skimp on proper procedure, 'shorten' reduces length, and 'trim' reduces by careful small cuts.

items.questionText: The route into the city was ____ by almost a mile when the new bridge opened.
items.explanation: 'Shorten' means to reduce in length or duration and is the neutral term. 'Cut corners' means to do a job improperly to save effort, 'save' would need a beneficiary, and 'trim' implies removing a small amount from the edges.

items.questionText: The board ____ the budget by four per cent across every department without redundancies.
items.explanation: 'Trim a budget' means to reduce it by modest, selective cuts. 'Cut corners' is an idiom about skimping on standards, 'save' needs someone to be spared something, and 'shorten' applies to length or duration rather than to sums of money.

items.questionText: The entire scheme rested on an elaborate ____ practised on elderly investors.
items.explanation: 'Deception' is the act of deliberately misleading someone. Spanish 'decepción' means 'disappointment', which is the false friend the original item turns on. 'Deceit' is the quality of being dishonest rather than a particular act, and 'delusion' is a false belief held by the person themselves.

items.questionText: He was dismissed for ____ rather than for any lack of competence.
items.explanation: 'Deceit' is the general quality or habit of dishonesty — an uncountable noun naming the vice itself. 'Deception' names a specific misleading act, 'delusion' is a mistaken belief one holds oneself, and 'disappointment' is the feeling that Spanish 'decepción' actually denotes.

items.questionText: He laboured for years under the ____ that the company was simply too large to fail.
items.explanation: 'A delusion' is a false belief the sufferer holds sincerely — note 'labour under a delusion' as the fixed frame. 'Deception' and 'deceit' both require someone doing the misleading, whereas a delusion needs no deceiver at all; 'disappointment' is a feeling of letdown.

items.questionText: Neither delegation was prepared to entertain the slightest ____ on the question of borders.
items.explanation: 'Compromise' means a settlement in which each side concedes something. Spanish 'compromiso' means 'commitment', which is the interference this quartet exploits. 'Commitment' is a binding undertaking, 'engagement' is an arrangement to meet, and 'implication' is a consequence.

items.questionText: She had a long-standing prior ____ that evening and sent her deputy in her place.
items.explanation: 'A prior engagement' is a fixed phrase for an appointment already in the diary. Spanish 'compromiso' covers this sense too, which is why the whole set blurs for learners: 'commitment' is a binding promise, and 'compromise' is a mutual concession.

items.questionText: The ____ of the ruling for smaller charities is a good deal graver than the judgment admits.
items.explanation: 'Implication' means a consequence that follows from something, or a meaning conveyed indirectly. Spanish 'implicación' can also mean 'involvement', which English 'implication' carries only in the phrase 'implication in a crime'. 'Commitment', 'compromise' and 'engagement' all concern undertakings, not consequences.

items.questionText: The shipyard struggled to recruit ____ welders at anything like short notice.
items.explanation: 'Skilled' describes practical expertise acquired through training and practice. 'Qualified' can mean formally certified but, before a noun such as 'support' or 'approval', means limited or hedged — that second sense is what the original item tested. 'Capable' means able, and 'conditioned' means trained to respond in a certain way.

items.questionText: She proved more than ____ of running the entire department single-handed.
items.explanation: 'Capable of' takes a gerund and means having the ability to do something. 'Qualified' would imply formal credentials, 'skilled' implies practised technique, and 'conditioned' implies a learned reflex — only 'capable' fits the 'of' pattern here.

items.questionText: Shoppers have been thoroughly ____ to expect next-day delivery as a matter of course.
items.explanation: 'Condition someone to do something' means to train them, through repeated experience, into an automatic expectation. 'Qualified' concerns credentials or hedging, 'skilled' concerns competence, and 'capable' concerns ability — none of them describes a learned reflex.

items.questionText: He is a patient and ____ supervisor, which is precisely why research students seek him out.
items.explanation: 'Understanding' as an adjective means sympathetic towards other people's difficulties — the sense Spanish 'comprensivo' has. 'Comprehensive' means complete in coverage, 'comprehensible' means able to be understood, and 'apprehensive' means anxious about what may happen.

items.questionText: The assembly instructions were barely ____ even to a qualified engineer.
items.explanation: 'Comprehensible' means capable of being understood — the property of the text, not of the reader. 'Comprehensive' means covering everything, 'understanding' describes a sympathetic person, and 'apprehensive' means uneasy; the three '-prehensive' forms are a classic C2 discrimination.

items.questionText: She grew steadily more ____ as the date of the disciplinary hearing drew closer.
items.explanation: 'Apprehensive' means anxious about something expected — its root is the 'apprehension' of dread, not of grasping. 'Comprehensive' means exhaustive, 'comprehensible' means intelligible, and 'understanding' means sympathetic.

items.questionText: The leaked correspondence proved deeply ____ to the minister's remaining prospects.
items.explanation: 'Damaging to' means harmful to something, and the preposition settles it. 'Damning' means proving guilt and modifies evidence directly rather than taking 'to'; 'condemning' means officially declaring unfit; and 'cursing' means swearing at.

items.questionText: The council served a notice ____ the building as unfit for human habitation.
items.explanation: 'Condemn a building' is the technical use: to declare it officially unfit. 'Damning' means proving someone guilty, 'damaging' means harmful and takes 'to', and 'cursing' means uttering oaths — only 'condemn' has this administrative sense.

items.questionText: He stumbled out into the rain, ____ his own carelessness under his breath.
items.explanation: 'Curse' here means to swear about something in anger. 'Damning' proves guilt, 'damaging' harms, and 'condemning' declares officially unfit; the shared idea of malediction is a trap, since 'damning' has lost that sense in modern usage.

items.questionText: Current rates of extraction are environmentally ____ over anything beyond the short term.
items.explanation: 'Unsustainable' means incapable of being kept up over time, and is the standard term in environmental and financial argument. 'Untenable' means impossible to defend against criticism, 'unbearable' means too painful to endure, and 'insupportable' is its formal literary twin.

items.questionText: The heat in the upper gallery had become quite ____ by the middle of the afternoon.
items.explanation: 'Unbearable' means too intense to be endured, and is the everyday word for physical discomfort. 'Untenable' concerns positions that cannot be defended in argument, 'unsustainable' concerns practices that cannot continue, and 'insupportable' is a far more formal synonym of 'unbearable'.

items.questionText: Such an imputation upon his honour was, to his mind, wholly ____.
items.explanation: 'Insupportable' is the formal, literary word for something that cannot be tolerated, and suits this elevated register where 'unbearable' would sound plain. Note that it does not mean 'unsupportable by evidence'; 'untenable' covers that, while 'unsustainable' means impossible to maintain over time.

items.questionText: She was a ____ woman who never in her life turned anyone away from the door.
items.explanation: 'Warm-hearted' describes a generous, kindly person. 'Lukewarm' describes an unenthusiastic response, not a person; 'cool-headed' describes calmness under pressure; and 'half-baked' describes an ill-considered plan.

items.questionText: It took a ____ negotiator to keep the talks alive through that final night.
items.explanation: 'Cool-headed' means calm and clear-thinking under pressure — a compliment, whereas the literal 'cool' would suggest indifference. 'Lukewarm' describes a tepid reception, 'warm-hearted' describes kindness, and 'half-baked' describes an unsound idea.

items.questionText: The whole proposal struck the committee as ____ and hopelessly under-costed.
items.explanation: 'Half-baked' means poorly thought out and not properly worked up. 'Lukewarm' describes a response rather than a plan, and 'warm-hearted' and 'cool-headed' both describe temperament — the baking metaphor is about incompleteness, not temperature.

items.questionText: He left academic life for ____ at the age of thirty-five and never returned.
items.explanation: 'Politics' is the activity and profession of government. Spanish 'política' covers both this and 'policy', which is exactly the split English forces you to make. 'Policy' is a stated course of action, 'polity' is an organised society or form of government, and 'police' is the force.

items.questionText: The essay compares the Athenian ____ with that of the Roman republic at its height.
items.explanation: 'A polity' is an organised political community or its form of government — a formal, largely academic term. 'Politics' is the activity, 'policy' is a course of action adopted, and 'police' is the law-enforcement body; only 'polity' names the constitutional entity itself.

items.questionText: The ____ were called shortly after midnight but found nothing out of place.
items.explanation: 'Police' is the law-enforcement force and takes a plural verb in British English. 'Policy' is a stated course of action, 'politics' the activity of government, and 'polity' a form of political organisation — the four are related only by their shared Greek root.

items.questionText: The crowd was already in ____ mood a full two hours before kick-off.
items.explanation: 'Exuberant' means overflowing with high spirits. Spanish 'exuberante' is used chiefly of vegetation and figures, so learners transfer it awkwardly; more importantly it must not be confused with 'exorbitant', which means unreasonably expensive. 'Exhaustive' means thorough and 'excruciating' means agonising.

items.questionText: The inquiry undertook an ____ review of every document the department still held.
items.explanation: 'Exhaustive' means leaving nothing out — do not confuse it with 'exhausting', which means tiring. 'Exorbitant' means far too expensive, 'exuberant' means high-spirited, and 'excruciating' means intensely painful.

items.questionText: The pain in his shoulder had become quite ____ by the third day without treatment.
items.explanation: 'Excruciating' means intensely painful, physically or (figuratively) socially. 'Exorbitant' means unreasonably high in price, 'exuberant' means brimming with energy, and 'exhaustive' means comprehensive — four 'ex-' adjectives that share nothing but their prefix.

items.questionText: Local businesses continue to ____ the festival with donations of both money and materials.
items.explanation: 'Support' here means to back something financially or materially. It does not mean 'to tolerate', which is where Spanish 'soportar' misleads; that sense needs 'bear' or 'put up with'. 'Weather' means to come safely through a difficult period, 'resist' means to withstand a temptation or force, and 'sustain' means to keep going.

items.questionText: Few of the delegates could ____ the temptation to check their phones during the address.
items.explanation: 'Resist a temptation' is the fixed collocation for refusing to give in to it. 'Weather' takes a storm or a crisis as its object, 'support' means to back or bear up, and 'sustain' means to maintain over time — none of them collocates with temptation.

items.questionText: The charity could not ____ that level of spending beyond a single financial year.
items.explanation: 'Sustain' means to keep something going at the same level over time. 'Weather' means to survive a bad period intact, 'support' means to bear or to back, and 'resist' means to withstand pressure — the emphasis in 'sustain' is on continuation rather than survival.

items.questionText: For all his obvious faults, he remained an oddly ____ figure to the very end.
items.explanation: 'Likeable' means easy to like — the meaning Spanish/Catalan 'simpático/simpàtic' actually carries. English 'sympathetic' means understanding of someone's plight, which is a quite different quality; 'pleasant' describes agreeableness in manner, and 'congenial' describes suitability to one's tastes.

items.questionText: We spent a thoroughly ____ afternoon in the walled gardens behind the house.
items.explanation: 'Pleasant' describes something enjoyable and agreeable, and applies to occasions as readily as to people. 'Sympathetic' means understanding towards someone's difficulty, 'likeable' applies only to people, and 'congenial' means suited to one's own temperament.

items.questionText: He found the atmosphere of the college unusually ____ to sustained scholarly work.
items.explanation: 'Congenial to' means well suited to a particular purpose or temperament, and the preposition 'to' is part of the pattern. 'Sympathetic' means understanding of a person, 'likeable' means easy to like, and 'pleasant' is a general term of approval that would not take 'to' this way.

items.questionText: One ____ exception to the pattern is the small northern colony, which has actually grown.
items.explanation: 'A notable exception' is fixed: 'notable' means worthy of attention. 'Notorious' means famous specifically for something bad, 'noted' means distinguished and normally precedes a person's field, and 'renowned' means widely celebrated.

items.questionText: She is a ____ authority on medieval canon law and has advised three governments.
items.explanation: 'A noted authority' is the standard collocation for someone eminent in a field. 'Notorious' would mean infamous, 'notable' means worth remarking on and suits things more than people, and 'renowned' is broader fame — 'noted' carries specifically scholarly distinction.

items.questionText: The region is ____ throughout Europe for the quality of its mountain cheeses.
items.explanation: 'Renowned for' means celebrated for something admirable. 'Notorious for' takes the same preposition but reverses the evaluation — it means famous for something bad, and that polarity is the whole point of this set. 'Notable' means worth remarking on, and 'noted' suits individual eminence.

items.questionText: The moor took on a ____, almost otherworldly quality in the failing light.
items.explanation: 'Weird' carries a suggestion of the uncanny or supernatural that the other options lack. 'Rare' means infrequent, not peculiar — Spanish 'raro' means both, which is the false friend here; 'strange' means unfamiliar, and 'odd' means not conforming to expectation.

items.questionText: She woke in a ____ room with no recollection whatever of having arrived there.
items.explanation: 'Strange' can mean simply unfamiliar — a room one does not know — a sense 'odd' and 'weird' do not have. 'Rare' means occurring infrequently, and Spanish 'raro' covering both 'rare' and 'strange' is precisely why learners misuse English 'rare' for oddness.

items.questionText: There were an ____ number of chairs, so somebody was always left standing.
items.explanation: 'Odd' has a mathematical sense — not divisible by two — that none of the other options shares, and the reference to someone standing confirms it. 'Rare' means infrequent, 'strange' means unfamiliar, and 'weird' means uncanny.

items.questionText: He ____ not to have noticed the error, which spared everybody a good deal of embarrassment.
items.explanation: English 'pretend' means to feign, to act as though something were true when it is not. Spanish 'pretender' means 'to intend', so the two are a two-way trap. 'Intend' states a purpose, 'attend' means to be present at, and 'contend' means to argue a case.

items.questionText: Barely a dozen members ____ the extraordinary general meeting called at such short notice.
items.explanation: 'Attend' means to be present at an event, and takes a direct object with no preposition — unlike Spanish 'asistir a'. 'Pretend' means to feign, 'intend' means to plan, and 'contend' means to argue or to compete.

items.questionText: Counsel ____ that the disputed clause had never been properly incorporated into the contract.
items.explanation: 'Contend that' means to argue a proposition against opposition — the natural verb in an adversarial hearing. 'Intend' concerns purpose, 'pretend' means to feign (never Spanish 'pretender'), and 'attend' means to be present at.

items.questionText: Very little of the lecture was ____ to anyone without a mathematical background.
items.explanation: 'Comprehensible' means able to be understood, and describes the thing being understood. 'Comprehensive' means covering everything, 'understanding' describes a sympathetic person, and 'sympathetic' means showing concern for someone's plight — the four are held apart by what each can modify.

items.questionText: Her employers proved unexpectedly ____ once she had explained the family situation.
items.explanation: 'Understanding' as an adjective means sympathetic and forgiving towards someone's difficulty — precisely what Spanish 'comprensivo' means, and precisely what English 'comprehensive' does not. 'Comprehensible' means intelligible, and 'sympathetic' overlaps but suggests feeling with someone rather than making allowances.

items.questionText: The review was broadly ____ to the book's aims, though it noted several weaknesses in execution.
items.explanation: 'Sympathetic to' means favourably disposed towards something. Learners reach for it when they mean 'likeable', because of Spanish 'simpático'. 'Comprehensive' means exhaustive, 'comprehensible' means intelligible, and 'understanding' describes indulgence towards a person rather than approval of a project.

items.questionText: The most ____ feature of the software is its habit of saving over your previous version.
items.explanation: 'Annoying' means causing mild irritation. It is the everyday sense that Spanish 'fastidioso' actually carries, which is why 'fastidious' is such a persistent false friend: in English it means meticulous about detail. 'Tedious' means boring, and 'bothersome' means causing minor trouble.

items.questionText: The transcription work was ____ in the extreme, but somebody had to do it.
items.explanation: 'Tedious' means tiresomely long and dull — the objection is to monotony, not to irritation. 'Fastidious' means painstakingly attentive to detail (not Spanish 'fastidioso'), 'annoying' means irritating, and 'bothersome' means causing inconvenience.

items.questionText: The damp patch in the corner is more ____ than genuinely serious.
items.explanation: 'Bothersome' means causing minor trouble or inconvenience, which the contrast with 'genuinely serious' confirms. 'Fastidious' describes a meticulous person, 'annoying' stresses irritation, and 'tedious' stresses dullness.

items.questionText: I can still ____ the smell of the workshop a good forty years afterwards.
items.explanation: 'Remember' means to retain and bring back to mind. 'Record' means to set down permanently — the sense the original item required, where sediments preserve evidence rather than recollect it. 'Recall' is the more formal act of retrieval, and 'remind' requires someone to be prompted.

items.questionText: Witnesses were asked to ____ the sequence of events in as much detail as they could.
items.explanation: 'Recall' means to bring something back to mind deliberately, and suits formal contexts where memory is being tested. 'Remember' is its everyday equivalent, 'record' means to register or set down, and 'remind' means to prompt somebody else's memory.

items.questionText: Could you ____ me to post the forms before five o'clock this afternoon?
items.explanation: 'Remind' always involves a second party: you remind someone of something. Spanish 'recordar' covers both remembering and reminding, which is why learners write 'remember me to post it'. 'Remember' and 'recall' are internal acts, and 'record' means to set down.

items.questionText: A surprisingly ____ proportion of applicants withdrew before the interview stage.
items.explanation: 'A large proportion' is the standard collocation for quantity expressed as a share. 'Long' measures extent in time or distance, 'wide' measures breadth, and 'grand' means imposing in scale or style — only 'large' pairs naturally with 'proportion'.

items.questionText: The river is nearly half a mile ____ where it opens into the estuary.
items.explanation: 'Wide' measures distance from side to side, which is what a river's span requires. 'Long' measures end to end, 'large' measures overall size, and 'grand' means impressive rather than dimensional — English keeps these measurements strictly separate where Spanish is more permissive.

items.questionText: The house was built on a ____ scale, with forty rooms and a chapel of its own.
items.explanation: 'On a grand scale' is fixed and means impressively large in conception. 'Long' and 'wide' are dimensional, and 'large' would state size without the connotation of magnificence that the sentence clearly wants.

items.questionText: Obtaining goods by ____ is a criminal offence quite distinct from theft.
items.explanation: 'Deception' is the deliberate act of misleading someone, and 'by deception' is fixed in legal usage. Spanish 'decepción' means 'disappointment', which is the false friend at work. 'Deceit' names the quality of dishonesty, and 'delusion' is a false belief held sincerely.

items.questionText: There was not a trace of ____ in anything she told the committee that morning.
items.explanation: 'Deceit' is an uncountable noun naming dishonesty as a quality or disposition, which is why 'a trace of' fits it. 'Deception' names a particular misleading act, 'delusion' is a mistaken belief, and 'disappointment' is the feeling Spanish 'decepción' denotes.

items.questionText: It is a widespread ____ that lightning never strikes the same place twice.
items.explanation: 'A delusion' is a false belief held in good faith, with nobody doing the deceiving. 'Deception' and 'deceit' both require a deceiver, and 'disappointment' is a feeling — the Spanish 'decepción' trap runs through this whole quartet.

items.questionText: Only two of the original frescoes ____ in anything approaching their original state.
items.explanation: 'Survive' means merely to continue to exist after a threat — no flourishing implied. 'Thrive' means to grow vigorously and prosper, which is the stronger claim the original item needed; 'persist' means to continue stubbornly, and 'endure' means to last, often through hardship.

items.questionText: If the symptoms ____ for more than a week, you should consult your doctor.
items.explanation: 'Persist' means to continue stubbornly, and is the standard verb for symptoms and problems that will not go away. 'Thrive' means to flourish, 'survive' means to remain in existence after danger, and 'endure' means to last or to bear patiently.

items.questionText: Few reputations ____ that degree of sustained public scrutiny entirely intact.
items.explanation: 'Endure' means to last through something difficult, with an emphasis on withstanding. 'Thrive' means to flourish, 'survive' means simply to remain alive or in existence, and 'persist' means to carry on obstinately rather than to withstand pressure.

items.questionText: The lettering on the memorial has ____ almost to the point of illegibility.
items.explanation: 'Fade' means to lose colour, brightness or clarity gradually. 'Dwindle' means to shrink in number or amount, 'melt' means to turn to liquid or to disappear gradually, and 'vanish' means to disappear abruptly and completely.

items.questionText: The last of the snow had ____ from the high corries by the middle of June.
items.explanation: 'Melt' is the literal verb for snow and ice turning to water. 'Dwindle' concerns diminishing quantity, 'fade' concerns loss of colour or intensity, and 'vanish' means to disappear suddenly and without trace.

items.questionText: The file ____ from the system without leaving so much as an entry in the logs.
items.explanation: 'Vanish' means to disappear suddenly and completely, which the absence of any trace confirms. 'Dwindle' implies gradual reduction, 'fade' implies gradual loss of intensity, and 'melt' implies a slow dissolving — all three are processes, whereas vanishing is an event.

items.questionText: He sat at the back of the class, ____ the end of his pencil and staring out of the window.
items.explanation: 'Chew' means to work something between the teeth repeatedly. 'Biting' as an adjective means bitterly cold or sharply sarcastic, 'gnaw' means to wear away by persistent biting, and 'nibble' means to take small delicate bites.

items.questionText: A ____ doubt about the wording of the indemnity kept him awake for most of the night.
items.explanation: 'Gnawing' figuratively describes a worry that persistently wears away at you. 'Biting' means either bitterly cold or cuttingly sarcastic, 'chewing' has no such figurative use, and 'nibbling' suggests something too slight to keep anyone awake.

items.questionText: Guests stood about ____ canapés and making determinedly polite conversation.
items.explanation: 'Nibble' means to eat in small, delicate bites, which suits the picture of half-hearted eating at a reception. 'Biting' implies force, 'chewing' implies sustained mastication, and 'gnawing' implies persistent wearing away.
