items.questionText: Fresh water was ____ at every stage of the route, so the party carried very little.
items.explanation: 'Plentiful' means available in ample supply. 'Torrential' applies only to rain and describes violence of flow, 'abundant' emphasises great quantity in existence, and 'generous' implies a giver — supply, quantity and giving are three different ideas.

items.questionText: The island supports an ____ birdlife found nowhere else in the archipelago.
items.explanation: 'Abundant' means existing in great quantity, and collocates naturally with wildlife and natural resources. 'Torrential' belongs to rain alone, 'plentiful' emphasises sufficiency of supply for a purpose, and 'generous' implies the act of giving.

items.questionText: The terms of the settlement were considerably more ____ than anyone had dared expect.
items.explanation: 'Generous' means giving more than is strictly required, and is used of terms, portions and offers. 'Torrential' describes rainfall, 'plentiful' describes supply, and 'abundant' describes sheer quantity — only 'generous' implies an agent choosing to give.

items.questionText: The company ____ a substantial loss on the venture in its very first year.
items.explanation: 'Make a loss' (and 'make a profit') is fixed. English distributes these delexical verbs unpredictably — you take a toll, do damage, have an effect and make a loss — so each pairing has to be learned rather than reasoned out from Spanish 'hacer'.

items.questionText: The storm ____ considerable damage to the roof of the west wing.
items.explanation: 'Do damage' is the fixed collocation — 'make damage' is one of the commonest Spanish-speaker errors, since 'hacer' covers both. 'Take a toll' is a separate idiom, 'make' pairs with losses and profits, and 'have' pairs with effects.

items.questionText: The intervention ____ remarkably little effect on the underlying rate of infection.
items.explanation: 'Have an effect' is fixed, as is 'have an impact'. 'Take a toll' means to cause cumulative damage, 'make' pairs with profits and losses, and 'do' pairs with damage and harm — four delexical verbs, four separate collocational fields.

items.questionText: The oak must be left to ____ for at least two years before it can be worked.
items.explanation: 'Season' as a verb means to dry timber gradually until it is fit for use. 'Weather' means to come through a difficult period, 'shower' means to bestow lavishly, and 'storm' means to attack a place — all four are weather nouns pressed into quite unrelated verbal service.

items.questionText: Well-wishers continued to ____ the couple with gifts for weeks after the ceremony.
items.explanation: 'Shower someone with something' means to give it in great abundance, and the preposition 'with' fixes it. 'Weather' takes a crisis as its object, 'season' means to dry or to flavour, and 'storm' means to take by force.

items.questionText: Demonstrators threatened to ____ the parliament building itself if the vote went ahead.
items.explanation: 'Storm a place' means to attack and capture it by sudden force. 'Weather' means to survive a difficult period, 'season' means to mature timber or flavour food, and 'shower' means to lavish something on someone.

items.questionText: It was an ____ solution, contrived from nothing but a length of wire and a paperclip.
items.explanation: 'Ingenious' means cleverly inventive. 'Ingenuous' — one letter away — means innocently frank and unsuspecting, and the pair is among the most treacherous in English. 'Disingenuous' means insincere while feigning candour, and 'genuine' means authentic.

items.questionText: It is frankly ____ to claim that the risks could not possibly have been foreseen.
items.explanation: 'Disingenuous' means pretending to be more naive or candid than one really is — an insincerity dressed as innocence. 'Ingenuous' means genuinely artless, 'ingenious' means cleverly inventive, and 'genuine' means real rather than counterfeit.

items.questionText: The dealer confirmed after examination that the signature was ____.
items.explanation: 'Genuine' means authentic, not forged. 'Ingenuous' means naively open, 'ingenious' means cleverly devised, and 'disingenuous' means falsely candid — only 'genuine' concerns authenticity of an object rather than a quality of character.

items.questionText: No ____ statement has yet been issued by the department on the matter.
items.explanation: 'Official' means authorised by, or issuing from, a body in authority. 'Officious' means interfering and self-important in the exercise of petty authority — a strongly negative word that Spanish 'oficioso' does not match. 'Efficient' means working without waste, and 'diligent' means industrious.

items.questionText: The new sorting system is markedly more ____ than the one it replaced, using half the staff.
items.explanation: 'Efficient' means achieving results with the minimum of wasted effort or resource. 'Official' means sanctioned by authority, 'officious' means meddlesome and self-important, and 'diligent' means conscientious in effort rather than economical in method.

items.questionText: A ____ researcher, he checked every citation against the original manuscript.
items.explanation: 'Diligent' means showing persistent and careful effort in one's work. 'Officious' would mean asserting petty authority over others, 'official' means authorised, and 'efficient' concerns economy of effort rather than thoroughness of it.

items.questionText: The descent in that visibility, with no rope between them, was frankly ____.
items.explanation: 'Terrifying' means causing intense fear. 'Terrific' has drifted right away from its root and now means excellent — which is exactly why it traps learners who expect it to mean 'terrible'. 'Terrible' means very bad in quality, and 'horrific' means causing horror and revulsion.

items.questionText: The acoustics in the old hall were ____, and half the audience heard almost nothing.
items.explanation: 'Terrible' in ordinary modern usage means very bad in quality. 'Terrific' means excellent — the same root, the opposite value; 'terrifying' means frightening, and 'horrific' means shockingly gruesome, which would be far too strong for poor acoustics.

items.questionText: The inspectors described conditions in the camp as ____ and demanded immediate closure.
items.explanation: 'Horrific' means causing horror through cruelty or suffering, and is reserved for genuinely shocking things. 'Terrific' means excellent, 'terrible' means merely very bad, and 'terrifying' stresses the fear induced rather than the moral shock.

items.questionText: After a short adjournment the tribunal will ____ at two o'clock this afternoon.
items.explanation: English 'resume' means to begin again after an interruption. Spanish 'resumir' means 'to summarise', so learners write 'resume the findings' when they mean 'summarise' them — the very trap the original item sets. 'Abridge' means to shorten a text, and 'condense' means to compress into less space.

items.questionText: The publisher asked her to ____ the text substantially for a schools edition.
items.explanation: 'Abridge' means to shorten a written work while preserving its substance, and is used almost exclusively of texts. 'Summarise' means to give the gist far more briefly, 'condense' means to compress into a smaller compass, and 'resume' means to start again after a break.

items.questionText: He somehow managed to ____ a three-hour discussion into a single page of notes.
items.explanation: 'Condense' means to compress something into a much smaller space while keeping its essentials. 'Summarise' would stress giving the main points, 'abridge' applies to shortening a published text, and 'resume' means to continue after an interruption — not Spanish 'resumir'.

items.questionText: The union will ____ a full public inquiry into the circumstances of the collapse.
items.explanation: 'Demand' means to insist on something forcefully. Spanish 'demandar' means 'to sue', which is exactly the false friend the original item exploits — English 'demand' has no legal sense at all. 'Denounce' means to condemn publicly, and 'claim' means to assert a right to something.

items.questionText: She was the first minister to ____ the practice publicly, and it cost her the whip.
items.explanation: 'Denounce' means to condemn something openly and vehemently. Spanish 'denunciar' also means 'to report to the police', a sense English 'denounce' lacks entirely. 'Sue' means to take legal action, 'demand' means to insist, and 'claim' means to assert entitlement.

items.questionText: Passengers may ____ compensation for any delay exceeding three hours.
items.explanation: 'Claim' means to apply for something one is entitled to. 'Sue' means to bring a lawsuit and takes the other party as its object, 'demand' means to insist forcefully without any implication of entitlement, and 'denounce' means to condemn publicly.

items.questionText: The mobile library was the first ____ of the latest round of budget cuts.
items.explanation: 'Casualty' means a victim or something lost as a result of an event. Spanish 'casualidad' means 'coincidence', which is the trap the original item sets — the two words look far closer than they are. 'Causality' means the relation of cause to effect, and 'eventuality' means a possible future occurrence.

items.questionText: A correlation of that kind establishes nothing whatever about ____.
items.explanation: 'Causality' is the principle that one thing brings about another — the abstract relation itself. 'Coincidence' means chance concurrence, 'casualty' means a victim, and 'eventuality' means a contingency; Spanish 'casualidad' pulls learners towards the wrong two of these.

items.questionText: The contract makes explicit provision for very nearly every conceivable ____.
items.explanation: 'An eventuality' is a possible future event, especially an unwelcome one that must be planned for. Beware Spanish 'eventual', which means 'temporary' or 'occasional'; English 'eventuality' has neither sense. 'Coincidence', 'casualty' and 'causality' concern chance, loss and cause respectively.

items.questionText: She writes ____ fiction set for the most part in the seventeenth century.
items.explanation: 'Historical' simply means relating to the past. 'Historic' means momentous enough to be remembered by history — the distinction is one of significance, not of period, and it is invisible in Spanish 'histórico'. 'Chronological' means arranged by time, and 'antiquated' means obsolete.

items.questionText: The letters have been arranged in strict ____ order rather than by correspondent.
items.explanation: 'Chronological' means ordered by time of occurrence. 'Historic' means momentous, 'historical' means pertaining to the past, and 'antiquated' means out of date — only 'chronological' describes a principle of arrangement.

items.questionText: The department still depends on an ____ filing system installed in the 1970s.
items.explanation: 'Antiquated' means obsolete and long overdue for replacement — an evaluative word, not merely a chronological one. 'Historic' means momentous, 'historical' means relating to the past, and 'chronological' means time-ordered.

items.questionText: The annual ____ attracts some two thousand delegates from more than forty countries.
items.explanation: A 'conference' is a large meeting of many speakers and participants. Spanish 'conferencia' means a single talk — an English 'lecture' — which is the false friend here. 'Lection' is a technical term in textual scholarship, and 'discourse' means extended discussion or a mode of speaking.

items.questionText: The editors compared each ____ preserved in the four surviving manuscripts.
items.explanation: 'Lection' is a narrow technical term in textual criticism for a variant reading of a passage — effectively its only surviving use. 'Lecture' is a talk, 'conference' is a large gathering, and 'discourse' is extended discussion; Spanish 'lección' means 'lesson', which fits none of them.

items.questionText: Public ____ has coarsened markedly over the past decade, on all sides alike.
items.explanation: 'Discourse' means the whole body of debate and communication on a subject. 'Lecture' is a single formal talk, 'conference' is a gathering, and 'lection' is a manuscript variant — 'discourse' alone names the collective activity rather than an event.

items.questionText: Marriage is a ____ that ought not to be entered into lightly by anyone.
items.explanation: 'Commitment' is a binding personal undertaking. Spanish 'compromiso' means exactly this, which is why learners then misuse English 'compromise' — that word means a settlement reached by mutual concession. 'Engagement' is an arrangement or betrothal, and 'concession' is what each side gives up.

items.questionText: Their ____ was announced in the paper the following Saturday morning.
items.explanation: 'Engagement' here is the betrothal — one of the senses Spanish 'compromiso' also covers, which is what makes this quartet so slippery. 'Commitment' is a binding undertaking, 'compromise' is a mutual concession, and 'concession' is a single thing conceded.

items.questionText: The government made one significant ____ to its own backbenchers before the vote.
items.explanation: 'A concession' is a specific point given up to placate the other side. 'Compromise' is the whole settlement that results from concessions on both sides, 'commitment' is a binding promise, and 'engagement' is an appointment or betrothal.

items.questionText: The liquid was so ____ that it barely moved when the flask was tilted right over.
items.explanation: 'Viscous' means thick and slow-flowing — a purely physical property. 'Vicious' means savage or cruel, and the two are separated by a single letter and constantly confused in writing. 'Malicious' means intending harm, and 'cyclical' means recurring in cycles.

items.questionText: The anonymous email was plainly ____ in intent and was reported to the police.
items.explanation: 'Malicious' means deliberately intending to cause harm — the emphasis is on intention. 'Vicious' stresses ferocity or savagery, 'viscous' means thick-flowing, and 'cyclical' means recurring at intervals.

items.questionText: Unemployment in the industry has always been strongly ____ rather than structural.
items.explanation: 'Cyclical' means recurring in regular cycles, and is the standard economic term. 'A vicious circle' is a fixed idiom for a self-worsening loop, which is why 'cyclical' looks tempting there but is quite wrong; 'viscous' means thick, and 'malicious' means spiteful.

items.questionText: The fleet is a rapidly ____ asset that the accounts have consistently overvalued.
items.explanation: 'Depreciate' means to fall in monetary value over time. 'Deprecate' means to express disapproval of, and survives chiefly in 'self-deprecating' — the two verbs are routinely confused because the spelling differs by two letters. 'Denigrate' means to blacken a reputation, and 'disparage' means to belittle.

items.questionText: He spent the entire address ____ his predecessor's record in office.
items.explanation: 'Denigrate' means to attack someone's reputation or character — its root is 'to blacken'. 'Deprecate' means to express disapproval, 'depreciate' means to lose value, and 'disparage' means to belittle the worth of something, more often a thing or quality than a person's good name.

items.questionText: She made several ____ remarks about the quality of the new translation.
items.explanation: 'Disparaging remarks' is a strong fixed collocation for comments that belittle something's worth. 'Denigrating' attacks a reputation more personally, 'deprecating' expresses disapproval and is now largely confined to 'self-deprecating', and 'depreciating' concerns loss of monetary value.

items.questionText: He was charged with being in charge of a vehicle while ____.
items.explanation: 'Intoxicated' is the formal and legal term for being under the influence of alcohol or drugs. Spanish 'intoxicado' means 'poisoned', which is the false friend the original item turns on. 'Inebriated' is a literary synonym for drunk, and 'contaminated' describes substances rather than people.

items.questionText: By midnight a good half of the wedding party were comfortably ____.
items.explanation: 'Inebriated' means drunk, and belongs to a jocular or literary register rather than a legal one — 'intoxicated' is the term a charge sheet would use. 'Poisoned' means harmed by a toxic substance, and 'contaminated' describes something made impure.

items.questionText: The entire batch had to be destroyed once the water supply was found to be ____.
items.explanation: 'Contaminated' means polluted by an unwanted substance, and describes things rather than people. 'Poisoned' implies actual toxic harm has been done, 'intoxicated' means under the influence of drink, and 'inebriated' means drunk — Spanish 'intoxicado' blurs the first and third.

items.questionText: ____ yourself to the panel briefly before you begin the presentation itself.
items.explanation: 'Introduce' means to make someone known to others, a sense no other option in this set has. 'Insert' means to put something physically into a slot or gap, 'enter' means to go into a place or to type in data, and 'input' belongs to data handling.

items.questionText: ____ the building by the side door, as the main entrance is kept locked after six.
items.explanation: 'Enter' means to go into a place, and takes the place as a direct object without a preposition. 'Insert' requires something to be put into a gap, 'introduce' means to present or make known, and 'input' concerns feeding data into a system.

items.questionText: ____ and output are handled by two entirely separate modules of the program.
items.explanation: 'Input' is functioning here as a noun, paired with 'output' — a use unavailable to the other three. 'Insert', 'enter' and 'introduce' are verbs of putting in, and none of them forms this standard technical pairing.

items.questionText: His ____ departure from the meeting startled everyone still sitting round the table.
items.explanation: 'Abrupt' means sudden and unexpected, often to the point of rudeness. 'Abject' means utter and degrading (abject failure, abject poverty), 'abstruse' means difficult to understand, and 'absolute' means complete or unconditional.

items.questionText: The central argument is far too ____ to be summarised in a single paragraph.
items.explanation: 'Abstruse' means obscure and hard to follow, especially in academic writing. 'Abject' means utterly wretched, 'abrupt' means sudden, and 'absolute' means total — only 'abstruse' describes difficulty of comprehension.

items.questionText: The chairman retains ____ discretion in the matter and need give no reasons.
items.explanation: 'Absolute' means complete and unqualified, and pairs naturally with 'discretion', 'majority' and 'power'. 'Abject' means utterly humiliating, 'abrupt' means sudden, and 'abstruse' means obscure — the shared 'ab-' prefix is the only thing linking them.

items.questionText: He was woken at three in the morning by the ____ of the telephone in the hall.
items.explanation: 'The ringing of' a telephone or bell is the noun form of the sound itself. 'Resounding' is an adjective meaning emphatic and unmistakable (a resounding defeat), 'sounding' appears mainly in 'sounding out' opinion, and 'echoing' describes sound reflected back.

items.questionText: The delegation is in Brussels ____ out opinion quietly ahead of the vote.
items.explanation: 'Sound out' is a phrasal verb meaning to investigate someone's views discreetly, and the particle 'out' is what identifies it. 'Resounding' means emphatic, 'ringing' describes a bell-like sound, and 'echoing' means reverberating.

items.questionText: Her footsteps came ____ down the length of the empty corridor.
items.explanation: 'Echoing' means reverberating, with the sound thrown back from surfaces. 'Resounding' is now almost always figurative and means emphatic, 'ringing' suggests a clear bell-like tone, and 'sounding' requires 'out' to mean anything in this frame.

items.questionText: The paper bears a faint ____ that is visible only when held against the light.
items.explanation: 'A watermark' is a design impressed into paper during manufacture, used to prove authenticity. 'A watershed' is a decisive turning point, 'a waterline' is where a hull meets the water, and 'a waterway' is a navigable channel.

items.questionText: The hull was scraped and repainted from the ____ upwards during the refit.
items.explanation: 'The waterline' is the level at which the surface of the water touches a vessel's hull. 'Watershed' means a decisive turning point, 'watermark' is an authentication mark in paper, and 'waterway' is a navigable route.

items.questionText: The canal remains the principal ____ linking the two industrial cities.
items.explanation: 'A waterway' is a river or canal used for transport. 'A watershed' is figuratively a turning point (and literally a drainage divide), 'a watermark' authenticates paper, and 'a waterline' marks a hull's depth in the water.

items.questionText: 'Synergy' was the inescapable ____ of every management seminar that decade.
items.explanation: 'A buzzword' is a fashionable term used more for effect than for meaning. 'A byword' is a name that has become synonymous with a quality, 'a watchword' is a guiding principle, and 'a password' grants access to a system.

items.questionText: Caution was the ____ throughout the closing stages of the negotiations.
items.explanation: 'A watchword' is a guiding principle adopted by a group. 'A byword' means a standing example of some quality, 'a buzzword' is a vogue term, and 'a password' is a security credential — all four combine 'word' with quite different second elements.

items.questionText: You will be prompted to change your ____ every ninety days without exception.
items.explanation: 'A password' is the secret string that authenticates a user. 'A byword' is a synonym for a quality, 'a buzzword' is a fashionable phrase, and 'a watchword' is a guiding maxim — only 'password' has this technical security sense.

items.questionText: A school of ____ was filmed circling the seamount at a depth of forty metres.
items.explanation: 'Hammerheads' are sharks named for the shape of their heads. 'At loggerheads' is a fixed idiom meaning in bitter disagreement, 'figureheads' are nominal leaders without real power, and 'spearheads' lead an attack or campaign.

items.questionText: The incoming directors turned out to be little more than ____, with no real authority at all.
items.explanation: 'Figureheads' are leaders in name only — the metaphor comes from the carved figure on a ship's prow, which leads but steers nothing. 'Loggerheads' occurs only in 'at loggerheads', 'hammerheads' are sharks, and 'spearheads' are those driving something forward.

items.questionText: She now ____ the campaign for greater transparency in party funding.
items.explanation: 'Spearhead' as a verb means to lead a campaign or attack from the front. 'Loggerheads' exists only in the idiom 'at loggerheads', 'hammerheads' are sharks, and 'figureheads' are precisely those who do not lead in any real sense.

items.questionText: He wore a ____ tie in the school colours, as he had every day for forty years.
items.explanation: 'Striped' means marked with parallel bands. 'Chequered' means marked in squares, and figuratively means containing both successes and disgraces — that second sense is what the original item tested. 'Mottled' means irregularly blotched, and 'dappled' means marked with soft patches of light and shade.

items.questionText: The plaster had gone ____ with damp all along the north wall of the chapel.
items.explanation: 'Mottled' means covered in irregular patches of different colours, usually through some defect or blemish. 'Chequered' means arranged in regular squares, 'striped' means banded, and 'dappled' implies a pleasing play of light rather than staining.

items.questionText: The path was ____ with sunlight falling through the beeches overhead.
items.explanation: 'Dappled' describes soft patches of light and shadow, and carries a distinctly pleasing connotation. 'Mottled' suggests blotching from damp or disease, 'chequered' means in regular squares, and 'striped' means in bands.

items.questionText: The book's central ____ are nowhere supported by anything resembling evidence.
items.explanation: 'Assertions' are confident statements presented as fact. 'Cast aspersions on' is a fixed idiom meaning to attack someone's reputation by insinuation, 'aspirations' are ambitions, and 'ascriptions' are attributions of authorship or cause.

items.questionText: Her ____ were never for one moment limited to the domestic stage.
items.explanation: 'Aspirations' are ambitions or hopes for the future. 'Aspersions' are damaging insinuations and appear only in 'cast aspersions on', 'assertions' are confident claims, and 'ascriptions' are attributions — four abstract nouns kept apart largely by their fixed verbs.

items.questionText: Several ____ of authorship in the older catalogue have since been overturned.
items.explanation: 'Ascriptions' are attributions of a work to a particular author or cause. 'Aspersions' are slurs cast on a reputation, 'assertions' are bare claims, and 'aspirations' are ambitions — only 'ascription' names the act of assigning something to a source.

items.questionText: The museum devotes an entire gallery to ____ life in the deep ocean.
items.explanation: 'Invertebrate' means lacking a backbone, and belongs strictly to biology. 'Inveterate' means long-established and habitual (an inveterate gambler), 'inveigling' means luring by flattery, and 'invective' is abusive language — the four share little beyond their opening syllable.

items.questionText: He succeeded in ____ his way onto the selection committee within a year of joining.
items.explanation: 'Inveigle one's way' means to worm into a position by persuasion or flattery. 'Inveterate' means confirmed by long habit, 'invertebrate' means spineless in the zoological sense, and 'invective' is abusive speech.

items.questionText: The open letter descended into pure ____ well before the end of the second page.
items.explanation: 'Invective' is sustained abusive language, and is uncountable. 'Inveterate' is an adjective meaning habitual, 'invertebrate' means without a backbone, and 'inveigling' means coaxing deceitfully — only 'invective' names a kind of writing.

items.questionText: The bank cultivated a determinedly ____ image, right down to the mahogany panelling.
items.explanation: 'Staid' means sedate, respectable and rather dull. 'Staunch' means firmly loyal, 'stagnant' means unmoving and going bad, and 'stark' means bleak or sharply defined — 'staid' is the only one that describes cultivated respectability.

items.questionText: Real wages in the sector have remained ____ for the better part of a decade.
items.explanation: 'Stagnant' means showing no growth or movement, with a suggestion of unhealthiness borrowed from standing water. 'Staunch' means steadfastly loyal, 'staid' means sedate, and 'stark' means severe or starkly evident.

items.questionText: The contrast between the two sides of the river is ____ and quite deliberate.
items.explanation: 'Stark' means severe and unmistakably sharp, and collocates strongly with 'contrast', 'choice' and 'warning'. 'Staunch' means loyal, 'staid' means sedately respectable, and 'stagnant' means static and stale.

items.questionText: New signings must run the ____ of press attention from their very first week.
items.explanation: 'Run the gauntlet' means to endure a sustained ordeal of criticism or attack. 'Run the gamut' means to cover the entire range of something — the two idioms share a verb and are constantly confused. 'Gambit' is an opening move, and 'gambol' means to frisk about.

items.questionText: The offer was plainly an opening ____ rather than a serious proposal.
items.explanation: 'A gambit' is an opening move calculated to gain an advantage, taken from chess. 'Gamut' is a complete range, 'gauntlet' belongs to 'run the gauntlet' or 'throw down the gauntlet', and 'gambol' means to leap about playfully.

items.questionText: Lambs ____ in the field below the house right through April.
items.explanation: 'Gambol' is a verb meaning to run and leap about in play — note the single 'l' distinguishing it from 'gamble'. 'Gamut' is a range, 'gauntlet' is a glove and by extension an ordeal, and 'gambit' is an opening manoeuvre.

items.questionText: Their friendship remained strictly ____ for the whole of the thirty years they knew each other.
items.explanation: 'Platonic' describes affection that is intimate but not sexual. 'Pyrrhic' describes a victory won at ruinous cost, 'Procrustean' means forcing things into an arbitrary uniform shape, and 'Panglossian' means absurdly optimistic — four adjectives from classical and literary sources with no overlap.

items.questionText: The new assessment framework is frankly ____, forcing every case into a single template.
items.explanation: 'Procrustean' alludes to the bandit who stretched or amputated his guests to fit his bed: it means enforcing uniformity with brutal disregard for difference. 'Pyrrhic' means ruinously costly, 'Platonic' means non-sexual, and 'Panglossian' means naively optimistic.

items.questionText: His ____ optimism survived even the third round of redundancies that autumn.
items.explanation: 'Panglossian' comes from Voltaire's Dr Pangloss, who insisted all was for the best in the best of all possible worlds: it means optimistic to the point of absurdity. 'Pyrrhic' means won at crippling cost, 'Platonic' means non-sexual, and 'Procrustean' means rigidly uniform.

items.questionText: The argument simply ____ the question it purports to be answering.
items.explanation: 'Beg the question' strictly means to assume the very point at issue. 'Beggar belief' means to be too extraordinary to be credible, 'belie' means to give a false impression of, and 'beckon' means to summon or to await invitingly.

items.questionText: Her perfectly composed manner ____ the anxiety she must have been feeling.
items.explanation: 'Belie' means to give a misleading impression of something, disguising the reality. 'Beggar' in 'beggars belief' means to exceed, 'beg' in 'beg the question' means to assume, and 'beckon' means to gesture someone forward.

items.questionText: A career at the Bar ____ for a good many of the brightest graduates.
items.explanation: 'Beckon' means to invite or summon, and figuratively describes a prospect that seems to await someone. 'Beggar' occurs in 'beggars belief', 'beg' in 'begs the question', and 'belie' means to misrepresent — only 'beckon' suggests an inviting future.

items.questionText: The tapes give ____ access to the negotiations exactly as they unfolded.
items.explanation: 'Unmediated' means direct, with nothing standing between observer and event. 'Unmitigated' means not lessened in severity and is almost always paired with disaster or nonsense, 'unmoderated' means without supervision, and 'unmatched' means unequalled.

items.questionText: The discussion forum was left entirely ____ and became unusable within months.
items.explanation: 'Unmoderated' means lacking anyone to supervise or filter contributions. 'Unmitigated' means unrelieved in severity, 'unmediated' means direct and unfiltered by any intermediary, and 'unmatched' means without equal.

items.questionText: Her command of the archival sources is ____ among scholars of the period.
items.explanation: 'Unmatched' means unequalled by anyone else. 'Unmitigated' means not made less severe, 'unmediated' means direct, and 'unmoderated' means unsupervised — the 'un-' prefix is all four have in common.

items.questionText: A ____ man by nature, he volunteered nothing whatever beyond what he was asked.
items.explanation: 'Taciturn' means habitually saying very little. 'Tacit' means understood without being stated and describes agreements rather than people, 'tactile' relates to the sense of touch, and 'tactful' means careful not to give offence.

items.questionText: The sculpture invites a ____ response quite as much as a visual one.
items.explanation: 'Tactile' means relating to the sense of touch. 'Tacit' means implied rather than spoken, 'taciturn' means uncommunicative, and 'tactful' means diplomatic — the near-identical openings hide four unrelated meanings.

items.questionText: It was a remarkably ____ way of telling him his services were no longer required.
items.explanation: 'Tactful' means showing sensitivity in handling a delicate matter. 'Tacit' means unspoken but understood, 'taciturn' means saying little, and 'tactile' concerns touch.

items.questionText: The party took a clean ____ of the northern constituencies for the first time in decades.
items.explanation: 'A clean sweep' means winning everything available. 'Hold sway' means to exercise dominant influence, 'a swing' is a measured shift in voting, and 'a swathe' is a broad strip of land or a large portion.

items.questionText: There was a pronounced ____ towards the incumbent in the closing week of the campaign.
items.explanation: 'A swing' is the measured shift of votes from one party to another — the standard term in electoral analysis. 'Sway' means dominant influence and appears in 'hold sway', 'sweep' means a total win, and 'swathe' means a broad band.

items.questionText: A broad ____ of farmland along the river was lost to the flooding.
items.explanation: 'A swathe' is a broad strip, originally the width cut by one sweep of a scythe. 'Sway' means influence, 'sweep' means a comprehensive win or a sweeping movement, and 'swing' means a shift of opinion.

items.questionText: Delegates were warned in advance not to ____ from the agreed text.
items.explanation: 'Stray from' means to wander away from a fixed path or brief. 'Err on the side of caution' is a fixed idiom, and 'err' alone means to make a mistake; 'lean towards' means to incline in favour of, and 'veer' means to change direction sharply.

items.questionText: The committee appears to ____ towards the second of the two options before it.
items.explanation: 'Lean towards' means to be inclined in favour of something without yet committing. 'Err' means to make an error, 'stray' means to wander from a path, and 'veer' implies an abrupt change of direction rather than a settled inclination.

items.questionText: The discussion began to ____ sharply away from the point actually at issue.
items.explanation: 'Veer' means to change direction abruptly, and the adverb 'sharply' confirms it. 'Err' means to go wrong, 'stray' means to wander gradually off course, and 'lean' means to incline in a settled direction.

items.questionText: The neighbourhood proved rather less ____ than the agent's description had implied.
items.explanation: 'Salubrious' means healthy and pleasant, and is used chiefly of places — often, as here, with dry understatement. 'Salutary' means beneficial as a corrective (a salutary lesson), 'salutatory' means relating to a greeting, and 'sanitary' concerns hygiene.

items.questionText: The dean opened proceedings with a brief ____ address to the incoming students.
items.explanation: 'Salutatory' means serving as a greeting — a rare and formal word. 'Salutary' means beneficially corrective, 'salubrious' means health-giving, and 'sanitary' relates to hygiene; the shared Latin root of health and greeting explains the whole cluster.

items.questionText: Poor ____ conditions in the camp were the immediate cause of the outbreak.
items.explanation: 'Sanitary' relates to hygiene and the disposal of waste. 'Salutary' means producing a beneficial corrective effect, 'salubrious' means health-giving and is used of places, and 'salutatory' means pertaining to a greeting.

items.questionText: Months of quiet diplomacy laid the ____ for the treaty eventually signed in Vienna.
items.explanation: 'Lay the groundwork' is fixed: to do the preparatory work that makes something later possible. 'A groundswell' is a build-up of public feeling, 'a grounding' is a basic training in a subject, and 'grounds' are reasons.

items.questionText: She has a thorough ____ in statistics as well as in economic theory.
items.explanation: 'A grounding in' a subject is a solid basic training in it. 'Groundwork' is preparatory work for a project, 'groundswell' is a surge of collective feeling, and 'grounds' are the reasons on which something rests.

items.questionText: The appeal was dismissed on purely procedural ____ without any hearing of the facts.
items.explanation: 'On the grounds of' something means for that reason, and the noun is plural in this legal frame. 'Groundwork' is preparation, 'grounding' is basic training, and 'groundswell' is a rising tide of opinion.

items.questionText: The cholera ____ of 1854 transformed the whole of British public health policy.
items.explanation: 'An epidemic' is an outbreak spreading rapidly through a population at a particular time. 'Endemic' means permanently present in a place, 'pandemic' means spread across many countries, and 'academic' means theoretical or of no practical consequence.

items.questionText: The influenza ____ of 1918 killed more people than the war that preceded it.
items.explanation: 'A pandemic' is an epidemic that has spread across continents. 'Epidemic' is confined to one population or region, 'endemic' means constantly present at a low level, and 'academic' means of theoretical interest only.

items.questionText: Whether the clause still applies is now purely ____, since the contract has lapsed.
items.explanation: 'Purely academic' is a fixed collocation meaning of no practical consequence. 'Endemic', 'epidemic' and 'pandemic' all describe the distribution of disease, and only 'academic' has this second, quite unrelated sense of theoretical irrelevance.

items.questionText: There is considerable ____ in rainfall between the two sides of the ridge.
items.explanation: 'Variation' means difference or fluctuation in degree. 'At variance with' is a fixed phrase meaning in conflict with — 'variance' outside that frame is a statistical term; 'variety' means a range of different kinds, and 'varying' is a participle needing a noun to modify.

items.questionText: The walled garden contains an extraordinary ____ of alpine plants.
items.explanation: 'A variety of' means a range of different types. 'Variance' means conflict (at variance with) or statistical dispersion, 'variation' means fluctuation in degree rather than diversity of kind, and 'varying' cannot follow an article.

items.questionText: The submissions were of ____ quality, some excellent and a good many dreadful.
items.explanation: 'Varying' is a participial adjective modifying a following noun — 'of varying quality' is a fixed frame. 'Variance' and 'variation' are nouns, and 'variety' would require 'of' before the thing varied, producing quite a different structure.

items.questionText: The potter ____ every bowl by hand on a traditional kick wheel.
items.explanation: 'Throw' is the technical verb for shaping clay on a potter's wheel. 'Throes' appears only in 'in the throes of' — a violent struggle or upheaval — and is a plural noun, while 'thrones' are royal seats and 'throngs' are crowds.

items.questionText: Both ____ passed to the same claimant within the space of a single year.
items.explanation: 'Thrones' are royal seats, and by extension the sovereignties they represent. 'Throes' means violent pangs and survives only in 'in the throes of', 'throws' is the verb of casting or shaping clay, and 'throngs' are large crowds.

items.questionText: Great ____ of visitors had gathered outside the cathedral by first light.
items.explanation: 'Throngs' are dense crowds of people. 'Throes' means agonising struggle, 'throws' is a verb form, and 'thrones' are royal seats — four near-homophones that a candidate must separate by sense alone.

items.questionText: The ledger is written throughout in a cramped nineteenth-century ____ hand.
items.explanation: 'Cursive' describes joined-up handwriting. 'Cursory' means hasty and superficial — the two look almost identical but describe a script and an inspection respectively; 'curt' means brusquely short in speech, and 'coarse' means rough in texture or manner.

items.questionText: His reply was so ____ that she assumed she must have offended him.
items.explanation: 'Curt' means rudely brief in speech or writing. 'Cursory' means done rapidly and without attention to detail, 'cursive' means written in joined-up script, and 'coarse' means rough or vulgar.

items.questionText: The sacks were made of a ____ material that chafed the skin badly.
items.explanation: 'Coarse' means rough in texture — and note the spelling against 'course', which is a homophone. 'Cursory' means superficial, 'cursive' means joined-up in handwriting, and 'curt' means abruptly brief.

items.questionText: The reservoir fell to a third of its capacity during the ____ of 1976.
items.explanation: 'A drought' is a prolonged period without rain. 'A dearth' is a scarcity of something, and takes 'of' plus the thing lacking; 'a deficit' is a shortfall in an account, and 'scarce' is an adjective that cannot follow 'the'.

items.questionText: The department is currently running a ____ of some four million pounds.
items.explanation: 'A deficit' is the amount by which expenditure exceeds income. 'A dearth' is a shortage of something in general and needs 'of', 'a drought' is a want of rain, and 'scarce' is an adjective.

items.questionText: Skilled labour became ____ almost overnight once the yard reopened.
items.explanation: 'Scarce' is the adjective for something in short supply, and is the only option here that can follow 'became'. 'Dearth', 'drought' and 'deficit' are all nouns naming the shortage rather than describing the thing that is short.

items.questionText: She ____ regularly with a research group based in Uppsala.
items.explanation: 'Collaborate with' means to work jointly with someone, and the preposition 'with' fixes it. 'Corroborate' means to confirm someone else's account and takes a direct object, 'correlate' means to show mutual statistical relation, and 'coordinate' means to organise several parts into a whole.

items.questionText: Household income ____ closely with life expectancy right across the sample.
items.explanation: 'Correlate with' means to vary in a consistent relation to something else — and famously does not establish cause. 'Corroborate' means to confirm testimony, 'collaborate' means to work jointly, and 'coordinate' means to bring into a harmonious arrangement.

items.questionText: A single duty officer ____ the response of all four emergency services.
items.explanation: 'Coordinate' means to organise separate elements so that they work together effectively. 'Corroborate' means to confirm an account with independent evidence, 'collaborate' means to work with someone, and 'correlate' means to show statistical association.

items.questionText: The appeal court ____ the original finding on every ground advanced.
items.explanation: 'Sustain' in legal usage means to uphold a finding or objection. 'Substantiate' means to prove with evidence, 'substitute' means to put one thing in place of another, and 'subsidise' means to support financially.

items.questionText: Margarine was routinely ____ for butter throughout the rationing years.
items.explanation: 'Substitute A for B' means to use A in place of B. 'Substantiate' means to support a claim with evidence, 'sustain' means to maintain or uphold, and 'subsidise' means to fund from public money — the shared 'sub-' prefix is the only real link.

items.questionText: The rural bus service is heavily ____ by the county authority.
items.explanation: 'Subsidise' means to support something financially so that it can be provided below cost. 'Substantiate' means to prove, 'sustain' means to keep going or to uphold, and 'substitute' means to replace.

items.questionText: The finding ____ an obvious difficulty for the standard account of the period.
items.explanation: 'Pose a difficulty', 'pose a threat' and 'pose a question' are all fixed. 'Posit' means to put forward as a premise for argument, 'impose' means to force something on someone, and 'depose' means to testify on oath or to remove from office.

items.questionText: The statute ____ a duty of care on every occupier of commercial premises.
items.explanation: 'Impose something on someone' means to place an obligation or burden on them by authority. 'Posit' means to assume for the sake of argument, 'pose' pairs with problems and questions, and 'depose' means to give sworn evidence.

items.questionText: The witness ____ that he was some forty miles away on the night in question.
items.explanation: 'Depose' means to testify on oath, typically in writing — a specialised legal sense quite separate from its other meaning of removing a monarch. 'Posit' advances a theoretical premise, 'pose' pairs with questions and threats, and 'impose' forces an obligation.

items.questionText: The inconsistency in his testimony badly ____ the rest of his account.
items.explanation: 'Undermine' means to weaken something gradually from below. 'Underpin' is its exact opposite — to support and strengthen — and the two are separated only by their second element; 'underline' means to emphasise, and 'undertake' means to commit to doing something.

items.questionText: The whole episode ____ just how fragile the arrangement had always been.
items.explanation: 'Underline' means to emphasise or draw attention to something. 'Underpin' means to provide the foundation for, 'undermine' means to weaken from beneath, and 'undertake' means to promise to carry out — four verbs built on 'under' with quite unrelated senses.

items.questionText: The contractor ____ to complete the works before the end of March.
items.explanation: 'Undertake to do something' means to give a formal commitment to do it, and takes a following infinitive. 'Underpin' means to support, 'undermine' means to weaken, and 'underline' means to emphasise — none of which can take an infinitive here.

items.questionText: All applications must ____ be submitted electronically and in a single file.
items.explanation: 'Henceforth' means from this moment onward. 'Hitherto' points the other way — up to now — 'thenceforth' means from that moment in the past, and 'hereafter' means later in this document or in the life to come.

items.questionText: The Act of Union was signed in 1707, and the two kingdoms were ____ one.
items.explanation: 'Thenceforth' means from that point in the past onward, and requires a past reference point — which the date supplies. 'Henceforth' means from now on, 'hitherto' means up until now, and 'hereafter' means later in the present text.

items.questionText: The two parties are ____ referred to as the Buyer and the Seller respectively.
items.explanation: 'Hereafter' means from this point onward in the present document — standard drafting language. 'Hitherto' means until now, 'henceforth' means from now on in time rather than in a text, and 'thenceforth' anchors to a past moment.

items.questionText: The wound was irrigated with a sterile ____ solution before being dressed.
items.explanation: 'Saline' means containing salt, and 'saline solution' is fixed in medicine. 'Salient' means standing out as most noticeable, 'sanguine' means cheerfully optimistic, and 'salutary' means beneficially corrective — a cluster held together only by their Latin openings.

items.questionText: He remains surprisingly ____ about the department's prospects for the coming year.
items.explanation: 'Sanguine' means cheerfully confident about the future — its old medical sense of blood-related survives only in etymology. 'Salient' means most prominent, 'saline' means salty, and 'salutary' means having a beneficial corrective effect.

items.questionText: A week without electricity proved a ____ experience for the entire household.
items.explanation: 'Salutary' means beneficial precisely because it is unpleasant — it corrects or teaches. 'Salient' means conspicuous, 'saline' means salty, and 'sanguine' means optimistic; note that 'salutary' does not mean 'healthy', which is 'salubrious'.

items.questionText: Fighting continued on a ____ basis for a further three months after the ceasefire.
items.explanation: 'Sporadic' means occurring at irregular and scattered intervals. 'Spurious' means false or not genuine, 'superfluous' means more than is needed, and 'scrupulous' means meticulously honest — the shared 's' opening is the whole of the resemblance.

items.questionText: Half the appendices are frankly ____ and could be cut without any loss.
items.explanation: 'Superfluous' means unnecessary because in excess of what is required. 'Spurious' means fake or based on false reasoning, 'sporadic' means intermittent, and 'scrupulous' means painstakingly principled.

items.questionText: She was ____ about acknowledging every last debt to earlier scholarship.
items.explanation: 'Scrupulous' means diligently attentive to what is right and proper. 'Spurious' means counterfeit, 'sporadic' means occurring irregularly, and 'superfluous' means surplus to requirements.

items.questionText: A ____ negotiator, she simply outlasted everyone else in the room.
items.explanation: 'Tenacious' means holding on firmly and refusing to give up. 'Tenuous' is its near-opposite in feel — thin, weak, barely holding — while 'tentative' means provisional and 'tenable' means capable of being defended.

items.questionText: The two sides reached a ____ agreement, subject in every respect to ratification.
items.explanation: 'Tentative' means provisional and not yet final. 'Tenuous' means insubstantial, 'tenacious' means persistent, and 'tenable' means defensible against objection — all four descend from Latin 'tenere', to hold, which is exactly why they blur.

items.questionText: That position is simply no longer ____ in the light of the new data.
items.explanation: 'Tenable' means able to be maintained or defended against criticism. 'Tenuous' means flimsy in substance rather than indefensible in argument, 'tentative' means provisional, and 'tenacious' means stubbornly persistent.

items.questionText: He ____ consulted his watch several times in the course of her speech.
items.explanation: 'Ostentatiously' means in a showy manner designed to be noticed — the point of the gesture is that everyone should see it. 'Ostensibly' means apparently but perhaps not really, and the two are constantly confused; 'obstinately' means stubbornly, and 'overtly' means openly.

items.questionText: The stain ____ refused to come out however hard she scrubbed at it.
items.explanation: 'Obstinately' means stubbornly, and is often used of inanimate things that resist our efforts. 'Ostensibly' means seemingly, 'ostentatiously' means in a deliberately showy way, and 'overtly' means openly and without concealment.

items.questionText: The campaign was ____ hostile to the incumbent from the very first week.
items.explanation: 'Overtly' means openly, with nothing hidden — the direct opposite of 'covertly'. 'Ostensibly' means apparently, and carries an implication that the appearance is false; 'ostentatiously' means showily, and 'obstinately' means stubbornly.

items.questionText: The film is determinedly ____ family entertainment with nothing to alarm anyone.
items.explanation: 'Wholesome' means morally or physically healthy and free from anything corrupting. 'Wholesale' means total and indiscriminate (wholesale reform), 'holistic' means treating something as an integrated whole, and 'whole-hearted' means completely committed.

items.questionText: The clinic takes a ____ approach, treating the patient rather than the presenting symptom.
items.explanation: 'Holistic' means considering the whole system rather than its parts in isolation. 'Wholesale' means sweeping and undiscriminating, 'wholesome' means healthy and morally sound, and 'whole-hearted' means unreserved in commitment.

items.questionText: The proposal has her ____ support and that of both her deputies.
items.explanation: 'Whole-hearted' means given without reservation, and describes commitment. 'Wholesale' means total and indiscriminate in scope, 'wholesome' means healthy and morally sound, and 'holistic' means treating something as an integrated whole.

items.questionText: He dismissed the objection in a ____ tone that plainly brooked no reply.
items.explanation: 'Peremptory' means insisting on obedience and allowing no discussion. 'Perfunctory' means done as a mere formality and without care — the two are close in spelling and wholly different in sense; 'preparatory' means preliminary, and 'precautionary' means taken as a safeguard.

items.questionText: Two full years of ____ work preceded the excavation itself.
items.explanation: 'Preparatory' means done in preparation for something that follows. 'Perfunctory' means carried out mechanically and without interest, 'peremptory' means imperiously final, and 'precautionary' means taken to guard against a risk.

items.questionText: The building was evacuated as a purely ____ measure while the alarm was checked.
items.explanation: 'A precautionary measure' is fixed: an action taken in advance to avert possible harm. 'Perfunctory' means done carelessly as a formality, 'peremptory' means brooking no dissent, and 'preparatory' means preliminary to something else.

items.questionText: It is a mere ____, but the dates in the second table do not match those in the first.
items.explanation: 'A cavil' is a petty objection raised over a trivial point. 'A caveat' is a substantive warning or qualification attached to a claim, 'caviar' is the delicacy, and 'a cavity' is a hollow space or a hole in a tooth.

items.questionText: The reception offered nothing more elaborate than ____ and very cold champagne.
items.explanation: 'Caviar' is salted sturgeon roe. It sits in this set purely as a spelling trap beside 'caveat', a formal warning or proviso; 'cavil' is a trifling objection, and 'cavity' is a hollow.

items.questionText: The dentist found a small ____ in one of the lower molars.
items.explanation: 'A cavity' is a hollow space, and in dentistry a hole caused by decay. 'A caveat' is a qualifying warning, 'a cavil' is a petty objection, and 'caviar' is a foodstuff — the shared 'cav-' opening is doing all the work here.

items.questionText: The ruling is widely regarded as a ____ judgment in the law of employment.
items.explanation: 'A landmark judgment' is one that marks a decisive change in the law. 'A hallmark' is a distinguishing characteristic, 'a benchmark' is a standard for comparison, and 'a watermark' authenticates paper.

items.questionText: The 1998 survey remains the ____ against which all later work is measured.
items.explanation: 'A benchmark' is a reference standard used for comparison, and 'against which' is its natural frame. 'A hallmark' is a defining quality, 'a landmark' is a turning point or prominent feature, and 'a watermark' is an authentication mark.

items.questionText: Each certificate carries a ____ that cannot be reproduced on any photocopier.
items.explanation: 'A watermark' is an image worked into paper during manufacture to prove authenticity. 'A hallmark' is an official stamp on precious metal and, figuratively, a defining characteristic; 'a landmark' marks a turning point, and 'a benchmark' is a standard of comparison.

items.questionText: She bought the painting on ____ and regretted it within the week.
items.explanation: 'On impulse' is fixed: acting on a sudden unreflecting urge. 'Impetus' is the driving force that gives momentum to a process, 'an imperative' is a pressing obligation, and 'impact' is the effect something has.

items.questionText: Reducing emissions is now a moral as well as an economic ____.
items.explanation: 'An imperative' is something that must be done — an obligation treated as beyond argument. 'Impetus' is momentum or driving force, 'impulse' is a sudden urge, and 'impact' is an effect.

items.questionText: The ____ of the ruling on smaller firms has yet to be properly assessed.
items.explanation: 'Impact on' means effect upon, and the preposition 'on' settles it. 'Impetus' means driving force and takes 'to' or 'for', 'impulse' means a sudden urge, and 'imperative' means a pressing obligation.

items.questionText: The ____ of the memorandum was clear enough, whatever its author now claims.
items.explanation: 'The purport' of a document is its apparent meaning or general sense. 'Purview' is the range of a body's authority or concern, 'a preview' is an advance viewing, and 'pursuit' is the act of chasing or of following an occupation.

items.questionText: Critics were given a ____ of the exhibition on the evening before it opened.
items.explanation: 'A preview' is an advance showing before general release. 'Purview' means the scope of someone's authority, 'purport' means the general sense of a document, and 'pursuit' means the act of chasing or of engaging in an activity.

items.questionText: He abandoned the law altogether for the ____ of a literary career.
items.explanation: 'The pursuit of' something means the sustained attempt to achieve it. 'Purview' is the extent of an authority's remit, 'purport' is the tenor of a document, and 'preview' is an advance viewing.

items.questionText: He was still walking with a ____ a full six months after the operation.
items.explanation: 'A crutch' is a support for walking, and figuratively anything one leans on too heavily. 'The crux' is the decisive point of a problem, 'the cusp' is the point of transition between two states, and 'a crust' is a hard outer layer.

items.questionText: The company is on the ____ of what may prove a decisive breakthrough.
items.explanation: 'On the cusp of' means at the point of transition into something. 'The crux' is the central difficulty of a question, 'a crutch' is a walking support, and 'a crust' is a hardened outer layer.

items.questionText: A thin ____ of ice had formed right across the surface of the tank.
items.explanation: 'A crust' is a hard outer layer that forms over something. 'The crux' is the essential point at issue, 'a crutch' is a support for walking, and 'the cusp' is a threshold between two states.

items.questionText: A short orchestral overture ____ the first act in the revised version.
items.explanation: 'Precede' means to come before in time or order. 'Preclude' means to prevent something from happening at all — the two differ by a syllable and by everything else; 'presume' means to assume without proof, and 'proceed' means to go forward.

items.questionText: The rule ____ that every member has read the standing orders in full.
items.explanation: 'Presume' means to take something for granted without verifying it. 'Preclude' means to rule out in advance, 'precede' means to come before, and 'proceed' means to continue or advance — the shared 'pre-' and 'pro-' openings are the whole trap.

items.questionText: The inquiry ____ on the assumption that the documents are authentic.
items.explanation: 'Proceed on' an assumption means to go forward taking it as given. 'Preclude' means to make impossible, 'precede' means to come before, and 'presume' means to suppose — note also the spelling trap with 'precede', which has no double 'e'.

items.questionText: The idea appears in ____ form in his earliest surviving notebooks.
items.explanation: 'Germinal' means in the earliest stage of development, like a seed. 'Germane' means relevant to the matter in hand, 'generic' means general rather than specific, and 'genuine' means authentic — four adjectives from three unrelated roots.

items.questionText: The pharmacy stocks the ____ version at roughly a quarter of the price.
items.explanation: 'Generic' means not protected by a trade name, and more broadly relating to a whole class rather than an individual. 'Germane' means pertinent, 'germinal' means embryonic, and 'genuine' means real as opposed to counterfeit.

items.questionText: There was ____ surprise on the faces of everyone round the committee table.
items.explanation: 'Genuine' means real and unfeigned. 'Germane' means relevant to the question at issue and normally takes 'to', 'germinal' means in an early formative stage, and 'generic' means belonging to a general class.

items.questionText: Recovery will be a long ____, and there are bound to be setbacks along the way.
items.explanation: 'A long road' is the idiomatic metaphor for a difficult process ahead. 'Par for the course' is a separate fixed idiom meaning entirely to be expected, 'route' implies a chosen way between two points, and 'path' suggests a narrower, often personal, way.

items.questionText: The safest ____ through the marshes had been marked out with poles.
items.explanation: 'Route' means the particular way chosen between two points, and is the natural word where selection between options is involved. 'Course' appears in 'par for the course' and in navigation, 'road' is a made way, and 'path' is a narrow track.

items.questionText: She chose a very different career ____ from the one her sister had followed.
items.explanation: 'Career path' is a fixed collocation. 'Course' would work in 'the course of her career' but not here, 'road' is used of long difficult processes, and 'route' implies a way between fixed points.

items.questionText: A ____ stripes are as individual as a human fingerprint.
items.explanation: Only one of these four possessives forms an idiom: 'the lion's share' means much the largest part. The rest are literal, and this item tests whether you can recognise a genuine animal reference rather than reaching for the idiom you half remember.

items.questionText: A ____ howl carried right across the frozen surface of the lake.
items.explanation: This is a literal possessive: the howl belongs to the wolf. 'The lion's share' is the only fixed idiom in the set, and learners who have met it often assume the other three must be idiomatic too — they are not.

items.questionText: A ____ paw print in the mud measured almost thirty centimetres across.
items.explanation: A literal possessive again. Note that English does have 'a bear market' and 'bear hug', but no idiom built on 'a bear's share' — only 'the lion's share' carries that sense of the largest portion.

items.questionText: Wild ____ return each autumn to spawn in the river where they hatched.
items.explanation: 'A red herring' is the idiom — a false clue that distracts from the real issue — and 'herring' has no literal role here. 'Salmon' is invariant in the plural and is the only fish in this set associated with spawning migration.

items.questionText: A ____ sky at dawn usually means rain before nightfall.
items.explanation: 'A mackerel sky' is the standard term for cloud mottled like the fish's markings — a genuine fixed phrase, unlike anything available with salmon or trout. 'A red herring' means a deliberate distraction, and is the idiom the original item tested.

items.questionText: The upper stream is stocked with brown ____ every spring.
items.explanation: 'Trout' is invariant in the plural and is the freshwater fish stocked in managed streams. 'Herring' belongs to 'a red herring', a misleading clue; 'salmon' migrates to spawn, and 'mackerel' gives its name to a mottled sky.

items.questionText: She warmed the ____ thoroughly before adding the leaves.
items.explanation: 'A storm in a teacup' is the idiom for a great fuss over a trivial matter, and the cup is what the phrase requires. Here the sense is literal: only the pot is warmed before the leaves go in.

items.questionText: Enforcing the rule against members is quite a different ____ of fish.
items.explanation: 'A different kettle of fish' means an entirely separate matter — a second idiom hidden in this set, and the reason 'kettle' cannot be dismissed as a literal distractor. 'A storm in a teacup' means a fuss about nothing.

items.questionText: He set the cup back down on its ____ without making a sound.
items.explanation: A 'saucer' is the small dish a cup stands on — a literal use. 'A storm in a teacup' is the idiom for exaggerated fuss, and 'a different kettle of fish' means a separate matter; neither 'saucer' nor 'teapot' carries any such figurative sense.

items.questionText: The dog had ____ the corner clean off the only surviving typescript.
items.explanation: 'Chew' means to work something repeatedly between the teeth, causing damage over time. 'Bite the bullet' is the idiom for facing something unpleasant with resolve, 'swallow' means to take down the throat, and 'grip' means to hold fast.

items.questionText: He ____ the insult without a word and carried on with his report.
items.explanation: 'Swallow an insult' means to accept it without retaliating. 'Bite the bullet' means to steel oneself for something painful, 'chew' means to grind between the teeth, and 'grip' means to seize — of the four, only 'swallow' takes an affront as its object.

items.questionText: The whole country was ____ by the trial for the best part of a fortnight.
items.explanation: 'Gripped by' means held in fascinated attention. 'Bite the bullet' is an idiom of endurance, 'chew' concerns mastication, and 'swallow' means to take down or to accept meekly — only 'grip' describes a hold on the attention.

items.questionText: Epiphany falls on the ____ day after Christmas, which is why the decorations come down then.
items.explanation: 'The eleventh hour' is the idiom — the last possible moment — and the number in it is fixed. Here the ordinal is literal and determined by the calendar; no other number will do.

items.questionText: A surprising number of hotels still have no ____ floor at all.
items.explanation: The reference is to the superstition around the number thirteen — a literal ordinal, not an idiom. 'The eleventh hour' means the very last moment; note that the idiom is fixed to eleven and cannot be adjusted.

items.questionText: The ____ chapter was written some years after the rest of the book.
items.explanation: 'Final' means last in a sequence. The trap is that 'the eleventh hour' means precisely 'at the last moment', so learners assume the two are interchangeable — but the idiom is fixed and 'the final hour' carries no such sense of a narrow escape.

items.questionText: A night's sleep helped him put the setback into some sort of ____.
items.explanation: 'Put something into perspective' means to see it in its true relative importance. 'Out of all proportion' means exaggerated beyond what is warranted, 'a measure of' means a certain amount of, and 'scale' means magnitude.

items.questionText: There was at least a ____ of truth in what he said, however clumsily he put it.
items.explanation: 'A measure of' means a certain amount of, and is the frame here. 'Proportion' appears in 'out of all proportion' meaning exaggerated, 'perspective' in 'put into perspective', and 'scale' means sheer size — each locked to its own preposition and article.

items.questionText: Nobody at the outset had grasped the sheer ____ of the undertaking.
items.explanation: 'The sheer scale of' something means its magnitude. 'Proportion' concerns relative size and appears in 'out of all proportion', 'perspective' concerns relative importance, and 'measure' means a quantity or degree.

items.questionText: He kept his ____ firmly shut for the whole of the disciplinary interview.
items.explanation: 'Pay lip service to' is the idiom — to express support one does not act on — and only 'lip' fits that frame. Here the reference is literal and physical, which is what makes 'mouth' the only possibility.

items.questionText: The whole remark was made entirely ____ in cheek, as everyone present understood.
items.explanation: 'Tongue in cheek' means said ironically, not meant seriously. 'Lip service' means empty professed support, 'a man of his word' means someone reliable, and 'mouth' has no such fixed idiom here — each body part belongs to exactly one phrase.

items.questionText: Whatever else you may say about him, he is a man of his ____.
items.explanation: 'A man of his word' means someone who keeps his promises. 'Lip service' is professed but hollow support, 'tongue in cheek' means ironically, and 'mouth' fits none of these fixed frames.

items.questionText: The children stood on ____ to see over the top of the wall.
items.explanation: 'On tiptoes' is literal — standing on the balls of the feet. 'On tenterhooks' is the idiom for anxious suspense (a tenter was a frame for stretching cloth), 'pinpoint' is a verb meaning to identify precisely, and 'hindsight' is knowledge after the event.

items.questionText: The report ____ three separate failures of supervision in the same department.
items.explanation: 'Pinpoint' as a verb means to identify something exactly. 'On tenterhooks' means in a state of nervous suspense, 'on tiptoes' is literal, and 'in hindsight' means with the benefit of later knowledge.

items.questionText: With ____, the warning signs that summer were entirely unmistakable.
items.explanation: 'With hindsight' means judging with knowledge acquired after the event. 'On tenterhooks' means in anxious suspense, 'on tiptoes' means stretched up on the feet, and 'pinpoints' is a verb of precise identification.

items.questionText: The ____ was left hopelessly exposed by a defence that had pushed too far forward.
items.explanation: 'Move the goalposts' is the idiom — to change the criteria once someone is already working to them — and only the posts appear in it. Here the reference is literal to the player between them.

items.questionText: The manager spent almost the entire second half pacing the ____.
items.explanation: 'The touchline' is the side boundary of the pitch, where the manager's technical area sits. 'Goalposts' belongs to the idiom 'move the goalposts', meaning to alter the rules unfairly; the other options are literal features of the ground.

items.questionText: The ____ still showed the wrong result a full ten minutes after the whistle.
items.explanation: 'The scoreboard' displays the score — a literal fixture of the stadium. 'Move the goalposts' is the only idiom available in this set, and it means changing the requirements after work has begun.

items.questionText: Nobody in the office trusts him, and with reason: he is thoroughly ____.
items.explanation: 'Two-faced' means hypocritical, saying one thing and meaning another. 'Double-edged' describes something with both a benefit and a drawback, 'twin-bladed' is literal and describes razors, and 'double-sided' describes printing or tape.

items.questionText: The razor's ____ head is what gives the closer shave.
items.explanation: 'Twin-bladed' is a purely literal compound: having two blades. 'Double-edged' is almost always figurative and means cutting both ways, 'two-faced' means hypocritical, and 'double-sided' describes something printed or coated on both faces.

items.questionText: The whole report was printed ____ in order to halve the paper used.
items.explanation: 'Double-sided' means using both surfaces of the sheet. 'Double-edged' means having both an advantage and a disadvantage, 'two-faced' means insincere, and 'twin-bladed' refers to a cutting head with two blades.

items.questionText: The playground has been fitted with new ____ and a climbing frame.
items.explanation: 'What you lose on the swings you gain on the roundabouts' is the idiom, and only 'roundabouts' completes it. Here the reference is literal playground equipment, which is exactly the discrimination the item tests.

items.questionText: The lecturer's ____ were far too crowded to read from the back of the hall.
items.explanation: 'Slides' here means projected presentation images — a second, quite separate sense from the playground apparatus. 'Swings and roundabouts' is the idiom for gains and losses balancing out, and neither 'seesaws' nor 'carousels' figures in it.

items.questionText: Baggage ____ three and four are both out of service this morning.
items.explanation: 'Carousel' has a technical airport sense — the revolving belt for luggage — alongside the fairground one. 'Swings and roundabouts' is the fixed idiom meaning that gains and losses cancel out, and 'roundabout' is the only one of the four that appears in it.

items.questionText: Whether the notice was served at all is a matter of ____ rather than of interpretation.
items.explanation: 'A matter of fact' contrasts with a matter of law or of opinion. 'A case in point' is the idiom for an illustrative example, 'out of the question' means impossible, and 'the matter in hand' means the business currently under discussion.

items.questionText: Reopening the whole inquiry at this stage is simply out of the ____.
items.explanation: 'Out of the question' means not to be considered — impossible. 'A case in point' means an apt illustration, 'a matter of fact' contrasts with interpretation, and 'the matter in hand' means the present business.

items.questionText: If we might return to the matter in ____, the deadline is on Friday.
items.explanation: 'The matter in hand' means the business currently before you. 'A case in point' is an illustrative instance, 'out of the question' means impossible, and 'a matter of fact' concerns what is objectively so — four idioms of reference held apart by their prepositions.

items.questionText: She filled a ____ at the pump and carried it back across the yard.
items.explanation: 'A pail' is a bucket. 'Beyond the pale' is the idiom for behaviour outside acceptable limits — from 'pale' meaning a boundary fence — and the two are homophones, which is precisely the trap. 'Pallor' means unhealthy paleness of the face, and 'palate' is the sense of taste.

items.questionText: The ____ of his face when he came in alarmed everybody in the room.
items.explanation: 'Pallor' is an unhealthy paleness of complexion. 'Beyond the pale' means outside the bounds of acceptable conduct, 'a pail' is a bucket, and 'the palate' is the roof of the mouth and hence the sense of taste.

items.questionText: The wine has a complexity that rewards a patient ____.
items.explanation: 'Palate' means the sense of taste, and by extension a person's discernment in food and wine. Distinguish it from 'palette' (an artist's board) and 'pallet' (a platform for goods); 'pale' belongs to 'beyond the pale', and 'pallor' means facial paleness.

items.questionText: Being genuinely bilingual gave her a clear ____ over the other candidates.
items.explanation: 'An advantage over' someone means a superior position relative to them, and the preposition 'over' fixes it. 'The benefit of the doubt' is a set phrase, 'in her favour' means to her advantage in a decision, and 'profit' means financial gain.

items.questionText: The tribunal's ruling went decisively in her ____ on every disputed point.
items.explanation: 'In someone's favour' means to their advantage in a decision or judgment. 'The benefit of the doubt' is a fixed phrase about withheld judgment, 'an advantage over' compares two parties, and 'profit' means monetary gain.

items.questionText: The gallery turned a small ____ for the first time in its eleven-year history.
items.explanation: 'Turn a profit' means to end up in financial surplus. 'The benefit of the doubt' means the presumption of innocence where evidence is lacking, 'advantage' is a superior position, and 'favour' means approval or preferential treatment.

items.questionText: Her ____ movement across the stage drew applause before she had spoken a word.
items.explanation: 'Graceful' means moving with elegance and poise — it describes physical bearing. 'Gracious' means courteous and generous in manner, 'grateful' means thankful, and 'gratuitous' means uncalled for; the shared root of 'grace' hides four quite separate meanings.

items.questionText: We are extremely ____ for all the help you have given us over the past year.
items.explanation: 'Grateful for' means feeling thankful, and the preposition 'for' fixes it. 'Gracious' describes the person conferring a kindness rather than the one receiving it, 'graceful' describes elegance of movement, and 'gratuitous' means unwarranted.

items.questionText: The violence in the second half of the film is entirely ____ and adds nothing.
items.explanation: 'Gratuitous' means done without good reason and therefore unjustified — note that its older sense of 'free of charge' survives only in 'gratuity'. 'Gracious' means courteous, 'graceful' means elegant, and 'grateful' means thankful.

items.questionText: The evidence, read fairly, simply does not ____ so sweeping a conclusion.
items.explanation: 'Support' here means to provide sufficient grounds for a claim. What it never means is 'to tolerate' — that is the sense of Spanish 'soportar', and the reason learners write 'I can't support him'. 'Abide' means to tolerate, 'sustain' means to keep going, and 'maintain' means to keep in repair or to assert.

items.questionText: It is very difficult to ____ that level of concentration for a full three hours.
items.explanation: 'Sustain' means to keep something going at the same level over time. 'Abide' means to put up with something disagreeable, 'support' means to bear or to corroborate, and 'maintain' means to keep in good order or to insist on a claim.

items.questionText: The trust is obliged to ____ the fabric of the building in good repair.
items.explanation: 'Maintain' means to keep something in proper condition — the sense in 'maintenance costs'. 'Abide' means to tolerate, 'support' means to bear weight or to corroborate, and 'sustain' means to keep going at a given level rather than to keep in repair.

items.questionText: The airline is now the largest ____ on the transatlantic route by some margin.
items.explanation: 'A carrier' is a company that transports passengers or goods. 'Career' means a professional life — Spanish 'carrera' covers both this and a university degree course, which is why the two English words are so often swapped. 'Course' is a route or a programme of study, and 'a cartel' is a price-fixing group.

items.questionText: The river has altered its ____ twice within living memory.
items.explanation: 'Course' means the path something follows. Spanish 'carrera' pushes learners towards 'career', which in English means a working life — though note the rare verb 'to career' does mean to move wildly. 'Carrier' is a transport company, and 'cartel' is a collusive group of producers.

items.questionText: The three producers operated an illegal ____ for the better part of a decade.
items.explanation: 'A cartel' is an association of producers who collude to control prices. 'Career' means a professional life, 'carrier' means a transport operator, and 'course' means a route or programme — the four are linked by nothing but their opening consonants.

items.questionText: The ____ of the second chapter is that the reforms were inevitable from the outset.
items.explanation: 'Argument' here means the line of reasoning a piece of writing advances. Spanish 'argumento' means the plot of a story, which is exactly the false friend the original item exploits. 'Subject' is what something is about, and 'topic' is a matter for discussion.

items.questionText: The ____ of the portrait has never been satisfactorily identified by scholars.
items.explanation: 'The subject' of a painting is the person or thing represented in it. 'Plot' means the sequence of events in a narrative, 'argument' means a line of reasoning (not Spanish 'argumento', which means plot), and 'topic' means a matter under discussion.
