items.questionText: The ____ of pension reform was carefully avoided throughout the evening.
items.explanation: 'A topic' is a subject of conversation or discussion. Note that Spanish 'tópico' means 'cliché', not 'topic' — a second false friend lurking in the same family. 'Plot' is a narrative structure, 'argument' is a reasoned case, and 'subject' is what something is about.

items.questionText: The seminar covered a remarkably wide range of ____ over the three days.
items.explanation: 'Topics' are matters discussed. Spanish 'tópicos' means 'clichés' — which is precisely what the original item required — so this pair traps learners in both directions. 'Themes' are recurring underlying ideas, and 'subjects' are what works or studies are about.

items.questionText: Exile and return are the recurring ____ of all her later poetry.
items.explanation: 'Themes' are the underlying ideas that recur through a body of work. 'Clichés' are worn-out phrases (Spanish 'tópicos'), 'topics' are matters discussed, and 'subjects' are what individual works depict — a theme runs through many works, a subject belongs to one.

items.questionText: Portrait painters generally prefer ____ who are capable of sitting still.
items.explanation: 'Subjects' here are the people depicted. 'Clichés' are stale expressions, 'topics' are matters for discussion, and 'themes' are recurring ideas; the Spanish 'tópico'/'cliché' overlap is what makes this whole set difficult.

items.questionText: He ____ the company outright after a disagreement over strategy.
items.explanation: 'Quit' means to leave a job or place, usually abruptly. 'Remove' means to take something off or away and needs an object that is being taken — 'remove one's shoes' — while 'retire' means to stop working at the end of a career, and 'withdraw' means to pull back from something.

items.questionText: She intends to ____ at the end of the academic year after thirty years in post.
items.explanation: 'Retire' means to give up work permanently on reaching the end of a career. Spanish 'retirarse' also covers simply withdrawing, which English splits off into 'withdraw'; 'quit' means to leave abruptly, and 'remove' requires a direct object.

items.questionText: Two of the five candidates chose to ____ before the ballot papers were printed.
items.explanation: 'Withdraw' means to pull out of a contest or process. 'Retire' means to end a working life, 'quit' means to leave abruptly, and 'remove' means to take something away and cannot be used intransitively of a person leaving.

items.questionText: The film ____ the two leads for the first time since 1994.
items.explanation: 'Reunite' means to bring together again people who have been apart, and takes a direct object. 'Meet' means simply to come together, 'rejoin' means to return to a body one previously belonged to, and 'reassemble' means to gather again as a group.

items.questionText: He ____ the firm next month after two years working abroad.
items.explanation: 'Rejoin' means to become a member of something again. 'Meet' means to come together, 'reunite' means to bring separated parties back together, and 'reassemble' is used of a body coming together again as a whole rather than an individual returning to it.

items.questionText: Parliament ____ in the second week of September after the summer recess.
items.explanation: 'Reassemble' is the formal verb for a body coming together again after an adjournment. 'Meet' is the neutral term for a regular session, 'reunite' means to bring separated people together, and 'rejoin' means to return to membership.

items.questionText: It had been an ____ year by any standard, and few were sorry to see it end.
items.explanation: 'Eventful' means full of incident. 'Eventual' means final, occurring at the end of a process — and neither means 'possible' or 'temporary', which is what Spanish 'eventual' conveys. 'Temporary' means lasting a limited time, and 'occasional' means happening now and then.

items.questionText: The arrangement is strictly ____ and will be reviewed again in June.
items.explanation: 'Temporary' means lasting only for a limited period — one of the senses Spanish 'eventual' carries, which is exactly why that word is such a reliable trap. 'Eventual' means final, 'eventful' means full of incident, and 'occasional' means intermittent.

items.questionText: He makes the ____ appearance at board meetings, and nothing more than that.
items.explanation: 'Occasional' means happening from time to time — the other sense Spanish 'eventual' covers. 'Eventual' means ultimate, 'eventful' means full of incident, and 'temporary' means short-lived; English distributes across four words what Spanish packs into one.

items.questionText: The ____ ran in every national paper for a full fortnight.
items.explanation: 'An advertisement' is a paid public notice promoting something. Spanish 'advertencia' means 'warning', which is the false friend the original item turns on. 'Advice' is a recommendation, and 'an announcement' is a public statement of fact.

items.questionText: She sought independent legal ____ before signing anything at all.
items.explanation: 'Advice' is a recommendation about what to do, and is uncountable — 'an advice' is always wrong. 'A warning' alerts to danger, 'an advertisement' promotes something commercially, and 'an announcement' states a fact publicly.

items.questionText: The ____ was made shortly after the markets had closed for the day.
items.explanation: 'An announcement' is a public statement of information. 'A warning' alerts to danger (Spanish 'advertencia'), 'an advertisement' is commercial promotion, and 'advice' is guidance on what to do — only 'announcement' is purely informational and one-off.

items.questionText: Fresh water is fast becoming the most fiercely contested ____ of all.
items.explanation: 'A commodity' is a raw material or primary good that is traded. Spanish 'comodidad' means 'comfort' or 'convenience', which is the false friend the original item exploits. 'Community' is a group of people, and 'commotion' is a noisy disturbance.

items.questionText: The entire ____ turned out for the funeral, shops closing for the afternoon.
items.explanation: 'A community' is a body of people living in one place or sharing an interest. 'Convenience' means ease and comfort (Spanish 'comodidad'), 'commodity' is a traded good, and 'commotion' is a noisy disturbance.

items.questionText: There was a considerable ____ in the corridor outside the committee room.
items.explanation: 'A commotion' is a noisy disturbance. 'Convenience' means comfort or ease of use, 'a commodity' is a traded good, and 'a community' is a group of people — four nouns whose shared 'comm-' opening is their only real connection.

items.questionText: The ____ at the foot of the will was subsequently shown to be a forgery.
items.explanation: 'A signature' is a person's name written by their own hand. 'Subject' can mean a school discipline or the person depicted in a work, 'an assignment' is a task set, and 'a matter' is an affair requiring attention.

items.questionText: The ____ is due at the end of the week and counts for a third of the module.
items.explanation: 'An assignment' is a piece of work set as part of a course. 'Subject' is the discipline itself rather than the task, 'signature' is a written name, and 'matter' is an affair or issue — Spanish 'asignatura' means 'subject', which is the trap here.

items.questionText: That is a ____ for the trustees rather than for this committee to decide.
items.explanation: 'A matter' is an affair or question requiring attention. 'Subject' is a field of study or what a work depicts, 'signature' is a written name, and 'assignment' is a task set — note that Spanish 'asignatura' points to 'subject', not to 'assignment'.

items.questionText: The proposal is still under ____ at committee level and no decision is expected.
items.explanation: 'Under discussion' means currently being talked over. 'An argument' is a reasoned case (or a quarrel), 'argumentation' is the abstract process of reasoning, and 'plot' is a narrative structure — Spanish 'discusión' means a quarrel, which is why learners misjudge the tone of this word.

items.questionText: The book's ____ is dense in places but never less than rigorous.
items.explanation: 'Argumentation' is the abstract process or manner of reasoning, and is uncountable. 'An argument' is a single reasoned case or a quarrel, 'discussion' is talk over a matter, and 'plot' is the storyline of a narrative.

items.questionText: The ____ of the film is very nearly impossible to summarise in a paragraph.
items.explanation: 'Plot' means the sequence of events in a story — which is precisely what Spanish 'argumento' denotes, making 'argument' the false friend to avoid here. 'Argument' in English is a reasoned case, 'argumentation' the process of reasoning, and 'discussion' is talk.

items.questionText: She ____ him a look across the table that ended the conversation at once.
items.explanation: 'Shoot someone a look' is fixed for a swift, pointed glance. 'Beam' means to transmit or to smile radiantly, 'shine' is intransitive and cannot take 'him a look', and 'cast' pairs with shadows, doubt and glances of a slower kind.

items.questionText: A single lamp ____ in the upstairs window long after midnight.
items.explanation: 'Shine' is intransitive here: the lamp emits light without an object. 'Beam' means to transmit a signal or to smile broadly, 'shoot' needs an object, and 'cast' requires something thrown — light, a shadow, or doubt.

items.questionText: The old elm ____ a long shadow right across the lawn by six in the evening.
items.explanation: 'Cast a shadow' is the fixed collocation — the verb means to throw something outward. 'Beam' means to transmit or to smile, 'shoot' implies sudden speed, and 'shine' is intransitive and cannot take 'a shadow' as its object.

items.questionText: The university is rapidly ____ its provision in the applied sciences.
items.explanation: 'Expand' is transitive here — the university expands something deliberately. 'Mounting' describes pressure or tension building of its own accord and is intransitive, 'swelling' suits crowds and volumes, and 'climbing' suits figures on a scale.

items.questionText: The crowd outside the embassy gates was ____ by the hour.
items.explanation: 'Swell' is the natural verb for a crowd growing in physical mass. 'Mounting' suits pressure, tension and criticism, 'expanding' suits deliberate enlargement of provision or territory, and 'climbing' suits measured figures.

items.questionText: Average temperatures have been ____ steadily since the middle of March.
items.explanation: 'Climb' is used of figures rising on a scale — temperatures, prices, indices. 'Mounting' describes abstract pressure accumulating, 'swelling' describes growth in bulk, and 'expanding' describes deliberate enlargement.

items.questionText: Prices are expected to ____ sharply once the subsidy is finally withdrawn.
items.explanation: 'Jump' is used of a sudden sharp rise in a figure. 'Skip a beat' is a fixed idiom about the heart, 'drop' means to fall, and 'lose' requires something to be lost — only 'jump' expresses an abrupt upward movement.

items.questionText: The temperature can ____ below freezing on that plateau even in May.
items.explanation: 'Drop' means to fall to a lower level. 'Skip' means to omit or, in 'skip a beat', to miss one; 'jump' means to rise sharply, and 'lose' needs an object such as 'heat' — the direction of movement is what separates them.

items.questionText: Try not to ____ your temper with them, however provoking they may be.
items.explanation: 'Lose one's temper' is fixed. 'Skip a beat' is a different fixed idiom, 'jump' means to rise or leap, and 'drop' means to fall — none of them collocates with 'temper'.

items.questionText: The warning was simply ____ by very nearly everyone who received it.
items.explanation: 'Disregard' means to pay no attention to something, often deliberately. 'Dismiss' means to reject it after explicitly judging it worthless, 'neglect' means to fail in a duty of care over time, and 'discard' means to throw away as no longer wanted.

items.questionText: The walled garden had been badly ____ for the best part of a decade.
items.explanation: 'Neglect' implies a failure to give something the care it was owed, over a stretch of time. 'Dismiss' is an act of judgment, 'disregard' is a refusal of attention, and 'discard' is a deliberate throwing away.

items.questionText: Several early drafts were ____ before he settled on the present opening.
items.explanation: 'Discard' means to get rid of something no longer wanted, and suits physical drafts. 'Dismiss' means to reject an idea as unworthy of consideration, 'disregard' means to ignore, and 'neglect' means to fail to maintain.

items.questionText: The varnish must be applied ____ across the whole of the surface.
items.explanation: 'Uniformly' means evenly, without variation from place to place. 'Invariably' means every single time — variation in time rather than in space — 'unanimously' means with everyone in agreement, and 'indiscriminately' means without making distinctions.

items.questionText: The motion was carried ____ and without any debate at all.
items.explanation: 'Unanimously' means with the agreement of every person voting. 'Invariably' means on every occasion, 'uniformly' means evenly throughout, and 'indiscriminately' means without discrimination between cases — only 'unanimously' concerns agreement among people.

items.questionText: The new levy falls ____ on rich and poor households alike.
items.explanation: 'Indiscriminately' means without distinguishing between cases that arguably deserve different treatment. 'Invariably' means always, 'uniformly' means evenly and without the critical edge, and 'unanimously' means with everyone's assent.

items.questionText: At its peak the union ____ some forty thousand workers across the region.
items.explanation: 'Represent' means to act formally on behalf of others. 'Depict' means to portray in a picture or narrative, 'exhibit' means to show a quality or put on display, and 'display' means to present for viewing.

items.questionText: The patient ____ none of the classic symptoms associated with the condition.
items.explanation: 'Exhibit' means to show or manifest a quality or symptom — the standard verb in clinical writing. 'Depict' means to portray artistically, 'represent' means to stand for or act on behalf of, and 'display' suggests deliberate showing.

items.questionText: The full results are ____ in the table on the following page.
items.explanation: 'Display' means to present information or objects so they can be seen. 'Depict' implies pictorial or narrative portrayal, 'represent' implies standing for something else, and 'exhibit' implies manifesting a quality.

items.questionText: The audience sat ____ throughout the whole ninety minutes without a murmur.
items.explanation: 'Enthralled' means held spellbound — its root is 'thrall', meaning bondage, so the sense is of being captured entirely. 'Absorbed' stresses concentration, 'captivated' stresses charm, and 'fascinated' stresses sustained interest.

items.questionText: She was quite ____ by the sheer elegance of the proof he had shown her.
items.explanation: 'Captivated by' means charmed and delighted — the attraction is to beauty or appeal. 'Absorbed in' means deeply concentrated on, 'enthralled' means held spellbound, and 'fascinated by' implies a more enduring intellectual pull.

items.questionText: He has been ____ by the mechanics of clocks since he was a small boy.
items.explanation: 'Fascinated by' describes a lasting intense interest in a subject, which the time reference confirms. 'Absorbed' describes momentary concentration and takes 'in', 'enthralled' means spellbound at a particular moment, and 'captivated' means charmed.

items.questionText: She ____ nervously at the clock, hoping the interview was nearly over.
items.explanation: 'Glance' means to look quickly and briefly, and takes 'at'. 'Peer' means to look hard at something difficult to make out, 'gaze' means to look long and steadily, and 'glare' means to stare angrily — the four differ in duration, effort and emotion.

items.questionText: The crowd ____ up at the painted ceiling in something close to silence.
items.explanation: 'Gaze' means to look long and steadily, typically in admiration or wonder. 'Peer' implies straining to see something indistinct, 'glance' is momentary, and 'glare' is hostile — only 'gaze' carries the note of absorbed contemplation.

items.questionText: He ____ at the interrupter until the whole room had fallen silent.
items.explanation: 'Glare' means to stare fiercely in anger or disapproval. 'Peer' means to look with effort at something hard to see, 'glance' means to look briefly, and 'gaze' means to look at length without any implication of hostility.
